Navigation World Models (Bar et al.) CVPR 2025 arXiv Camera-controlled video prediction for planning
V-JEPA 2: Self-Supervised Video Models Enable Understanding, Prediction and Planning (Assran et al.) arXiv 2025 arXiv The JEPA line behind entries 27 and 39
VGGT: Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer (Wang et al.) CVPR 2025 arXiv The feed-forward 3D reconstruction trend behind entries 20, 21 and 28
π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control (Black et al.) RSS 2025 arXiv The VLA family that Splat2Act (29) personalizes

Learning resources

  • Finding papers yourself. arXiv “new” listings for cs.GR, cs.CV, cs.RO and cs.HC; the arXiv API for date-restricted queries (the exercise below uses it); Ke-Sen Huang’s conference paper lists for SIGGRAPH, SIGGRAPH Asia, EG, HPG and EGSR.
  • Reading a paper quickly. Read the abstract, then the teaser figure, then the method overview figure, then the limitations. The “what / how / new / connection” structure of this digest is a template you can use for your own notes.
  • Background on this blog. The chapters linked from each entry. The figure scripts for this issue (bin/figures/paper-digest/) and the data file data/01-papers.json are in the site repository.

Exercises

  1. Form factors. Using the form_factor function from entry 19, place patch $j$ at $(0, y, 2)$ but tilt its normal toward the origin, $n_j = -(0,y,2)/\lVert(0,y,2)\rVert$. How does $F_{i\to j}(y)$ now fall off with $y$? Plot both curves.
    Hint

    Now $\cos\theta_j = 1$, so only one cosine shrinks, as $2/r$. The fall-off becomes $2A_j/(\pi r^3)$ instead of $4A_j/(\pi r^4)$, which is slower.

  2. Features instead of colours. Take the 3DGS compositing formula $C(p)=\sum_k T_k\,\alpha_k G_k(p)\,c_k$ and replace $c_k\in\mathbb{R}^3$ by $f_k\in\mathbb{R}^{16}$. What changes in the rasterizer’s memory traffic and in the backward pass? Which entries of this issue rely on this trick?
    Hint

    Only the per-Gaussian payload and the accumulation buffer grow, from 3 to 16 channels; sorting, tiling and the transmittance $T_k$ are unchanged. The gradient with respect to $f_k$ is $T_k\alpha_k G_k(p)$ times the upstream gradient, exactly as for colour. Entries 21, 28 and 33 use this trick.

  3. Engine or generator? For a simple game such as Pong, list which parts of the state you would keep in an explicit engine and which you would leave to a video generator, following Matrix-Game 4.0 and BoxWorld. What would an Orbia-style revisit test reveal for an end-to-end model?
    Hint

    Keep the ball and paddle positions, the score and the collision rules in the engine, because they must be exact and persistent. Leave textures, lighting and particle effects to the generator. An end-to-end model may “forget” the score or the court layout when the camera returns.

  4. Stochastic transparency. Three Gaussians lie along a ray with opacities $0.5, 0.4, 0.6$ and colours $1, 0, 1$ (grey levels), front to back. Compute the alpha-blended colour. Then show that keeping each Gaussian with probability $\alpha_k$ and taking the nearest kept one (black if none is kept) has the same expected value.
    Hint

    Blended: $0.5\cdot1 + 0.5\cdot0.4\cdot0 + 0.5\cdot0.6\cdot0.6\cdot1 = 0.5 + 0.18 = 0.68$. In the stochastic version the probability that Gaussian $k$ is the nearest kept one is $\alpha_k\prod_{l<k}(1-\alpha_l)$, which is exactly its blending weight $T_k\alpha_k$, so the expectations match. SteadySplats (entry 9) attacks the variance of this estimator.

  5. Make your own digest entry. Use the arXiv API, for example http://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=cat:cs.GR+AND+submittedDate:[202611010000+TO+202611302359], to find one November 2026 paper, and write the four parts (what, how, new, connection to CG) in at most 150 words.

The next issue will cover November to December 2026.
entry.summary: Issue 01 of the dated paper digest: 42 verified papers first posted between 1 October and 2 November 2026, in six categories, each with what it does, how it works, what is new and how it connects to computer graphics.

entry.title: Learning roadmap: from computer graphics to 3D Gaussian Splatting, world models and embodied AI

link.title: Learning roadmap: from computer graphics to 3D Gaussian Splatting, world models and embodied AI

entry.content:
This post is the map for the rest of the blog. I am a PhD student working at the intersection of embodied AI, world models, AR/VR, HCI and computer graphics, and these fields share one surprisingly linear story: learn how images are formed (graphics), learn how to invert that process from photos (neural rendering, 3D Gaussian Splatting), learn models that predict how the world evolves (world models), and finally put a body inside the world and let it act (embodied AI).

The blog is organised as five series that follow that story, plus a dated paper-digest column. Four series are the stages of the story itself; the fifth, on graphics engines, is the bridge between them, because the simulators that train robots and the neural game engines that world models are becoming are both engines underneath. Every post comes in English, Chinese and Japanese, with the math written out, small runnable code snippets and links to representative papers from SIGGRAPH, CVPR/ICCV/ECCV, NeurIPS/ICLR/ICML, CoRL/RSS and other top venues. Each track also has a curated reading list in the repository.

flowchart TB
  P[Prerequisites<br/>linear algebra, probability,<br/>Python / C++, PyTorch] --> G
  subgraph G[1. Computer graphics]
    direction LR
    G1[Math and transforms] --> G2[Rasterization] --> G3[Shading] --> G4[PBR] --> G5[Path tracing] --> G6[Real-time RT]
    G4 --> G7[Simulation]
    G2 --> G8[Geometry processing]
    G7 --> G9[Animation]
    G5 --> G10[Volumes]
    G5 --> G12[Differentiable rendering]
    G6 --> G11[Real-time techniques]
    G11 --> G13[2026 frontiers]
    G12 --> G13
  end
  G --> N
  subgraph N[2. Neural rendering]
    direction LR
    N1[Cameras and SfM] --> N2[NeRF] --> N3[Fast radiance fields] --> N4[3D Gaussian Splatting] --> N5[3DGS frontiers] --> N6[Capture to VR]
  end
  N --> X
  subgraph X[2.5 Graphics engines: the bridge]
    direction LR
    X1[Engine anatomy] --> X2[GPU APIs and render graphs] --> X3[Mini engine] --> X4[Production engines] --> X5[Physics and simulation engines] --> X6[AI meets engines]
  end
  X --> W
  subgraph W[3. World models]
    direction LR
    W1[Model-based RL] --> W2[Generative models] --> W3[Video world simulators] --> W4[3D/4D world generation] --> W5[JEPA and evaluation]
  end
  W --> E
  X --> E
  subgraph E[4. Embodied AI]
    direction LR
    E1[Robotics basics] --> E2[RL for robots] --> E3[Simulation] --> E4[Imitation learning] --> E5[VLA models] --> E6[Embodied AI x XR/HCI]
  end

Stage 0: prerequisites

You do not need everything below before starting, but you will meet all of it:

  • Linear algebra: vectors, matrices, eigen-decomposition, SVD. Much of graphics and vision is $4\times 4$ matrices and least squares.
  • Calculus and probability: integrals over the hemisphere, expectations, Monte Carlo estimation $\hat I = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i f(x_i)/p(x_i)$, Gaussians.
  • Programming: Python with NumPy and PyTorch for most posts; some GLSL and C++ for rendering.

Stage 1: computer graphics from scratch

How an image is made: from transforms and rasterization to physically based light transport and simulation. This is the foundation for everything that follows: NeRF is volume rendering, 3DGS is a differentiable rasterizer, and robot simulators are physics engines plus renderers. Chapters 1-7 are the core. Chapters 8-13 go deeper into geometry, animation, volumes, real-time techniques and differentiable rendering, and end with a survey of the 2026 research frontier; you can read them now or come back to them after the later stages.

  1. Roadmap and the math toolkit
  2. Rasterization
  3. Shading and textures
  4. Physically based rendering
  5. Ray tracing and path tracing
  6. Real-time ray tracing
  7. Physically based simulation
  8. Geometry processing: meshes, curvature, smoothing, subdivision and reconstruction
  9. Animation and characters: splines, rotations, skinning, IK, motion matching and learned motion
  10. Volumes and participating media: fog, smoke, clouds, sky and skin
  11. Real-time rendering techniques: G-buffers, soft shadows, AO, reflections, real-time GI and tone mapping
  12. Differentiable and inverse rendering: gradients through pixels
  13. Graphics research frontiers 2026: what SIGGRAPH, SIGGRAPH Asia and the latest preprints are doing

Stage 2: neural rendering and 3D Gaussian Splatting

Inverting the rendering process: recover cameras from photos, then fit a radiance field (NeRF) or a set of 3D Gaussians (3DGS) that reproduces them. These representations are now the backbone of 3D capture for AR/VR and of many 3D world-generation systems.

  1. Cameras and multi-view geometry
  2. NeRF
  3. Fast radiance fields
  4. 3D Gaussian Splatting
  5. 3DGS frontiers
  6. From capture to VR: a hands-on tutorial

Stage 2.5: graphics engines (the bridge)

A renderer becomes a world that agents can live in only once it sits inside an engine: a game loop, scene data, GPU resources, physics and tools. This series opens up that machinery, from the anatomy of an engine and modern GPU APIs to a mini WebGPU engine you build yourself, the production engines behind games and VR, and the physics engines that double as robot simulators. It ends where the next two stages begin: robot simulators are engines, and neural game engines are world models.

  1. Anatomy of a game engine: loops, data, ECS, jobs and tools
  2. Modern GPU APIs and render graphs
  3. Build a mini engine: WebGPU, glTF, PBR, shadows and an ECS in the browser
  4. Inside production engines: Unreal Engine 5, Unity 6, Godot 4, Bevy and others
  5. Physics and simulation engines: from game physics to robot simulators
  6. AI meets graphics engines: neural rendering, generative content and neural game engines

Stage 3: world models

From reconstructing the world to predicting it: latent dynamics models for planning, the generative toolkit (VAEs, diffusion, flow matching, transformers), video world simulators such as Genie, explicit 3D/4D world generation, and the JEPA view of predictive representation learning.

  1. What is a world model?
  2. Generative modeling foundations
  3. Video world simulators
  4. 3D and 4D world generation
  5. JEPA, evaluation and open problems

Stage 4: embodied AI

Giving the model a body: kinematics and control, reinforcement learning and sim2real, simulators, imitation learning, vision-language-action models, and finally how embodied AI connects with XR and human-computer interaction.

  1. Robotics foundations
  2. Reinforcement learning for robots
  3. Simulation platforms
  4. Imitation learning
  5. Vision-language-action models
  6. Embodied AI meets XR and HCI

Suggested pace

Stage Posts Suggested time Milestone
Graphics 13 8-11 weeks (core 1-7: 4-6 weeks) write a software rasterizer and a small path tracer
Neural rendering 6 3-4 weeks train 3DGS on your own capture and view it in VR
Graphics engines 6 3-5 weeks build a mini WebGPU engine with a render graph and profile a frame
World models 5 3-4 weeks train a tiny latent dynamics model or DDPM
Embodied AI 6 4-6 weeks train a policy in simulation from demonstrations

Play with it

The home page has an interactive lab with demos written for this blog: a GPU path tracer (GGX, NEE + MIS, à-trous denoising), Gaussian World (an editable, relightable open world of 3D Gaussians), XPBD cloth simulation, and eye-tracked foveated rendering. The posts link to the relevant demo wherever it helps.

Keeping up with new papers

The series explain the foundations; the dated paper digest column keeps them current. Each issue covers a fixed date window and collects recent papers in six categories (graphics, graphics engines and real-time, neural rendering, world models, embodied AI, and HCI/XR), each with what it does, how it works, what is new and how it connects to the series. The first issue, October-November 2026, covers 42 papers first posted between 1 October and 2 November 2026.

Browse by category

Graphics · Neural rendering · Graphics engines · World models · Embodied AI · Paper digest

I will keep extending these series as I learn; corrections and suggestions are very welcome.
entry.summary: The map of this blog: five series plus a dated paper-digest column, in order, with what to learn at each stage.

entry.title: Embodied AI meets XR and HCI: humans as data, operators and partners

link.title: Embodied AI meets XR and HCI: humans as data, operators and partners

entry.content:
Why this matters

Every post in this series has quietly depended on people. Demonstrations for imitation learning come from human teleoperators; VLAs are pre-trained on human-made web data and fine-tuned on human-collected robot data; world models learn from videos that people recorded; and the end goal is robots that work with and for people. Extended reality (XR: VR, AR and mixed reality) and human-computer interaction (HCI) are the disciplines that study exactly these interfaces between humans and machines. After VLA models, this final post looks at the human side of embodied AI in four roles: the human as a source of motion data, as a teleoperator, as a collaborator, and as a user of interfaces such as digital twins. It ends with research opportunities at the intersection of embodied AI, world models, AR/VR, HCI and graphics.

Prerequisites

  • Posts 1 (SE(3) transforms, IK), 4 (imitation learning and data collection) and 5 (VLAs, world models).
  • Basic familiarity with VR/AR headsets (6-DoF tracking, hand tracking, passthrough).
  • Graphics background helps for the sections on body models, rendering and digital twins.

1. Capturing human motion

Sensors

Technology Examples What it measures Trade-offs
Optical marker mocap Vicon, OptiTrack 3-D marker positions, sub-millimetre studio only, occlusions, markers on the body
Inertial suits Xsens-style IMU suits segment orientations portable, drift in global position
Markerless vision multi-view or monocular pose estimation body and hand keypoints, mesh fits cheap, less accurate, struggles with occlusion
XR headsets Quest, Vision Pro, Project Aria head 6-DoF, hands (26 or so joints), eye gaze egocentric, real time, limited body tracking
Gloves and wearables data gloves, tactile gloves, EMG bands finger angles, contact pressure, muscle activity richest hand data, intrusive

Parametric body and hand models

Raw keypoints are noisy and incomplete, so graphics-style parametric models are fitted to them. SMPL (Loper et al. SIGGRAPH Asia 2015) represents a body mesh with shape parameters $\beta$ and pose parameters $\theta$ (axis-angle rotations of 24 joints):

\[M(\beta, \theta) = W\big(T_P(\beta, \theta),\, J(\beta),\, \theta,\, \mathcal{W}\big), \qquad T_P(\beta, \theta) = \bar T + B_S(\beta) + B_P(\theta),\]

where $\bar T$ is a template mesh, $B_S$ and $B_P$ are learned linear shape and pose-corrective blend shapes, $J(\beta)$ regresses joint locations, and $W$ is linear blend skinning with weights $\mathcal{W}$: each vertex is transformed by a weighted sum of the joints’ rigid transforms $G_k(\theta, J) \in SE(3)$,

\[v_i' = \sum_{k} w_{ik}\, G_k(\theta, J)\, v_i .\]

The $G_k$ are exactly the forward-kinematics chain of post 1: a human body model is a kinematic tree with a skin. MANO (Romero et al. SIGGRAPH Asia 2017) does the same for hands, and SMPL-X combines body, hands and face. AMASS (Mahmood et al. ICCV 2019) unified many mocap datasets into SMPL parameters; it is the standard source of human motion for training humanoid controllers.

Linear blend skinning is easy to see on a 2-D strip with two bones:

Retargeting human motion to robots

Human and robot bodies differ in link lengths, joint limits and degrees of freedom, so motion has to be retargeted. The usual formulation is an optimization per frame:

\[q^{\ast}_t = \arg\min_{q} \sum_{k} \left\lVert s\, p^{\text{human}}_k - p^{\text{robot}}_k(q) \right\rVert^2 + \lambda_1 \lVert q - q^{\ast}_{t-1}\rVert^2 \quad \text{s.t. } q_{\min} \le q \le q_{\max},\]

matching selected keypoints (wrists, elbows, fingertips) with a scale $s$ while staying smooth and within joint limits. It is solved with the damped least-squares IK of post 1 or a small QP. For dexterous hands, matching fingertip relative vectors (thumb-to-index distance) matters more than absolute positions, because pinch grasps depend on it. Whole-body retargeting for humanoids adds balance: H2O and OmniH2O (He et al. 2024) retarget AMASS motions to a humanoid, filter infeasible ones, and train an RL tracking policy in simulation; HumanPlus (Fu et al. CoRL 2024) trained such a “shadowing” policy on about 40 hours of human motion data and then let a humanoid copy a person’s body and hand motion in real time from a single RGB camera, using the shadowing data for imitation learning.

Two small experiments show both halves of this paragraph: keypoint retargeting of an arm, and why relative fingertip vectors matter for a pinch.

2. Egocentric data: learning from how people see and act

Humans perform manipulation tasks billions of times a day, and egocentric (first-person) video captures them from a viewpoint close to a robot’s head or wrist camera.

  • Ego4D (Grauman et al. CVPR 2022): 3,670 hours of daily-life video from 931 camera wearers in 74 locations across 9 countries, with benchmarks for episodic memory, hand-object interaction and forecasting.
  • Ego-Exo4D (CVPR 2024): synchronized egocentric and exocentric views of skilled activities, with 3D body and hand poses.
  • Project Aria (Meta, 2023): research glasses with an RGB camera, two SLAM cameras, two eye-tracking cameras, IMUs, a seven-microphone array and more, plus machine-perception services (SLAM trajectories, eye gaze, hand tracking). Aria Digital Twin (ICCV 2023) pairs Aria recordings with a full digital reconstruction of the scene and objects, giving ground-truth 3D for every frame.
  • EgoDex (Apple, ICLR 2026): 829 hours of egocentric video recorded with Apple Vision Pro, with paired 3D hand and finger tracking for 194 tabletop manipulation tasks.

How robots use it:

  1. Visual representations. R3M (Nair et al. CoRL 2022) pre-trained a visual encoder on Ego4D with time-contrastive and video-language objectives and improved data efficiency of downstream robot imitation.
  2. Plans and priors from human play. MimicPlay (Wang et al. CoRL 2023) learns a high-level latent plan from cheap human play videos and a low-level controller from a small amount of teleoperation.
  3. Human data as robot data. EgoMimic (Kareer et al. ICRA 2025) records humans wearing Aria glasses and treats human hand trajectories as another embodiment, co-training with robot data; DexCap (Wang et al. RSS 2024) uses a portable mocap glove plus a chest camera to collect dexterous hand data that is retargeted to robot hands.
  4. Latent actions from video, as in Genie and GR00T’s data pyramid (post 5), turn action-free video into training signal.

The embodiment gap remains the central challenge: human hands are not grippers, and human videos show the human, not the robot. Masking or inpainting the hand, retargeting to robot kinematics, and matching camera viewpoints (head camera ≈ robot head camera, wrist camera ≈ UMI) are the main tricks.

The viewpoint argument is geometric. Projecting the same tabletop into a head-mounted and a wrist-mounted pinhole camera shows how different the two observations are:

3. VR and AR teleoperation for data collection

Since robot learning is bottlenecked by demonstrations, the teleoperation interface determines both data quantity and quality. XR headsets are attractive because they already track the head and hands at high rates, are cheap, and show stereo video.

flowchart LR
  H[Operator in headset] -->|head, hand poses 60-90 Hz| M[Mapping: calibration, clutch, retargeting]
  M -->|EE targets / joint targets| R[Robot controller]
  R --> C[Robot cameras: stereo head cam, wrist cams]
  C -->|video stream| H
  R --> D[Dataset: observations + actions]
  C --> D

Representative systems:

  • VR teleoperation for deep imitation (Zhang et al. ICRA 2018) showed early that consumer VR can collect demonstrations for visuomotor policies.
  • Holo-Dex (Arunachalam et al. ICRA 2023) and AnyTeleop (Qin et al. RSS 2023) map tracked human hands to multi-fingered robot hands, with AnyTeleop supporting many arms and hands from a vision-based hand tracker.
  • Open-TeleVision (Cheng et al. CoRL 2024) streams stereoscopic video from a head-mounted camera that actively follows the operator’s head, giving immersive first-person perception; on Unitree H1 and Fourier GR1 humanoids, stereo streaming improved success and completion time, and the active camera made control faster and smoother.
  • Bunny-VisionPro (Ding et al. IROS 2025) adds haptic feedback and collision avoidance for bimanual dexterous teleoperation with Apple Vision Pro.
  • GELLO (Wu et al. IROS 2024) is the low-cost alternative: 3D-printed kinematic replicas of the robot arm, showing that joint-space leader-follower devices are often more precise than free-space hand tracking.

Engineering the mapping

The core of any XR teleoperation system is a chain of SE(3) transforms (post 1) plus some HCI. A typical design:

  • Calibration $T_{\text{robot},\text{headset}}$ between the headset’s tracking frame and the robot base (from a marker, a shared anchor, or manually aligning a virtual robot with the real one in passthrough).
  • Clutching (relative mapping): when the operator holds a button, the current hand and end-effector poses are stored, and subsequent hand motion is applied relative to them. The operator can release, move the hand back to a comfortable spot and re-engage, as with lifting a mouse.
  • Motion scaling for precision (e.g. 2:1) and filtering of tracking jitter. The 1€ filter (Casiez, Roussel and Vogel, CHI 2012), a classic from HCI, is a first-order low-pass filter whose cutoff rises with speed, so it removes jitter when the hand is still and lag when it moves fast.
import numpy as np

class OneEuroFilter:
    """1 Euro filter (Casiez, Roussel, Vogel, CHI 2012): a speed-adaptive low-pass filter.
    Slow motion -> low cutoff (removes jitter); fast motion -> high cutoff (removes lag)."""
    def __init__(self, freq, min_cutoff=1.0, beta=0.05, d_cutoff=1.0):
        self.freq, self.min_cutoff, self.beta, self.d_cutoff = freq, min_cutoff, beta, d_cutoff
        self.x_prev, self.dx_prev = None, None

    def _alpha(self, cutoff):
        tau = 1.0 / (2 * np.pi * cutoff)
        return 1.0 / (1.0 + tau * self.freq)

    def __call__(self, x):
        if self.x_prev is None:
            self.x_prev, self.dx_prev = x, np.zeros_like(x)
            return x
        dx = (x - self.x_prev) * self.freq
        a_d = self._alpha(self.d_cutoff)
        dx_hat = a_d * dx + (1 - a_d) * self.dx_prev               # filtered speed
        cutoff = self.min_cutoff + self.beta * np.linalg.norm(dx_hat)
        a = self._alpha(cutoff)
        x_hat = a * x + (1 - a) * self.x_prev
        self.x_prev, self.dx_prev = x_hat, dx_hat
        return x_hat

def pose(R=np.eye(3), p=np.zeros(3)):
    T = np.eye(4); T[:3, :3] = R; T[:3, 3] = p
    return T

def rot_z(a):
    c, s = np.cos(a), np.sin(a)
    return np.array([[c, -s, 0], [s, c, 0], [0, 0, 1]])

class ClutchTeleop:
    """Relative (clutched) mapping from a VR hand/controller pose to a robot end-effector target.
    T_robot_headset is a calibration transform (headset tracking frame -> robot base frame)."""
    def __init__(self, T_robot_headset, scale=1.0):
        self.T_rh, self.scale = T_robot_headset, scale
        self.anchor_hand = self.anchor_ee = None

    def engage(self, T_h_hand, T_r_ee):             # clutch pressed: remember both poses
        self.anchor_hand = self.T_rh @ T_h_hand      # hand pose expressed in the robot frame
        self.anchor_ee = T_r_ee.copy()

    def target(self, T_h_hand):
        T_r_hand = self.T_rh @ T_h_hand
        dp = (T_r_hand[:3, 3] - self.anchor_hand[:3, 3]) * self.scale   # scaled translation
        dR = T_r_hand[:3, :3] @ self.anchor_hand[:3, :3].T              # rotation since engage
        return pose(dR @ self.anchor_ee[:3, :3], self.anchor_ee[:3, 3] + dp)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    freq = 90.0                                          # headset tracking rate (Hz)
    t = np.arange(0, 3, 1 / freq)
    # the operator moves the hand 20 cm along x in the headset frame, with 3 mm tracking jitter
    true = np.stack([0.2 * np.clip(t - 1, 0, 1), 0 * t, 0 * t], 1) + np.array([0.3, 1.2, -0.4])
    noisy = true + rng.normal(0, 0.003, true.shape)

    T_rh = pose(rot_z(np.pi / 2), np.array([0.5, 0.0, -0.8]))   # headset frame -> robot base
    teleop = ClutchTeleop(T_rh, scale=0.5)              # 2:1 motion scaling for precision
    ee0 = pose(p=np.array([0.4, 0.0, 0.3]))
    teleop.engage(pose(p=noisy[0]), ee0)
    f = OneEuroFilter(freq, min_cutoff=1.0, beta=5.0)
    raw = np.array([teleop.target(pose(p=x))[:3, 3] for x in noisy])
    filt = np.array([teleop.target(pose(p=f(x)))[:3, 3] for x in noisy])
    still = t < 1.0                                      # hand at rest
    print("jitter at rest  raw %.2f mm, filtered %.2f mm" %
          (1e3 * raw[still].std(0).max(), 1e3 * filt[still].std(0).max()))
    moving = (t > 1.0) & (t < 2.0)
    print("max |filtered - raw| while moving: %.1f mm" % (1e3 * np.abs(filt[moving] - raw[moving]).max()))
    print("final target", np.round(filt[-1], 3), "(expected [0.4, 0.1, 0.3])")

jitter at rest  raw 1.61 mm, filtered 0.42 mm
max |filtered - raw| while moving: 6.9 mm
final target [0.4   0.099 0.299] (expected [0.4, 0.1, 0.3])

The 3 mm tracking noise becomes 1.6 mm after 2:1 scaling and about 0.4 mm after the 1€ filter, while the 20 cm hand motion along the headset’s $x$ axis correctly becomes 10 cm along the robot’s $y$ axis (the calibration rotates by 90°). The deviation while moving (about 7 mm, including the noise the raw signal still carries) is the lag the filter trades for smoothness; beta sets that trade-off, and tuning it with real users is an HCI experiment in itself. The resulting target poses go to the IK or impedance controller of post 1.

Both effects, the frame change and the filtering, are easier to judge in pictures of the same run:

Human factors

XR teleoperation is a human-factors problem as much as a robotics one:

  • Latency. Motion-to-photon latency in the headset and command latency to the robot add up; above roughly 100 ms operators slow down and overshoot, and mismatched head motion and video cause discomfort. Predictive display and local reprojection of the robot’s video (as in VR timewarp) help.
  • Embodiment and presence. Seeing the robot’s hands where one’s own hands are (first-person, stereo, correct scale) makes teleoperation intuitive; mismatched scale or viewpoint breaks it.
  • Haptics. Most XR teleoperation is purely visual. Vibration cues, force feedback from leader arms, or visual force overlays reduce excessive grasp forces.
  • Workload and data quality. NASA-TLX workload, task time and success rate are standard HCI measures; for learning, demonstration consistency and smoothness matter too, because they affect the policy (post 4).
  • Rendering budget. High-resolution stereo streams are expensive. Eye-tracked foveated rendering, shading at full resolution only where the user looks, is one way to cut the cost of photoreal digital twins in the headset.

4. Human-robot interaction

Once robots work near people, interaction quality matters as much as task success:

  • Legibility and predictability. Dragan, Lee and Srinivasa (HRI 2013) distinguished predictable motion (what an observer expects given the goal) from legible motion (which lets an observer infer the goal quickly), and showed how to optimize trajectories for legibility. Exaggerating motion toward the intended object makes intent readable.
  • Shared autonomy. The robot infers the user’s goal from partial input (a joystick, gaze, EEG) and assists, blending user commands with autonomous actions. Gaze from XR headsets is a strong intent signal.
  • Communicating intent. AR can show the planned trajectory, the object the robot will grasp, or a safety zone, which is often clearer than robot motion or lights alone.
  • Safety and trust. Collaborative robots limit power and force (ISO/TS 15066 gives body-region limits); learned policies need runtime monitors and safe fallback controllers. Calibrated trust, neither over- nor under-reliance, is a core HCI concern.
  • Language interaction. VLAs make language the default interface, which raises classic HCI questions: ambiguity, clarification dialogues, and explaining failures.

5. Digital twins and mixed-reality interfaces

A digital twin is a synchronized virtual copy of the robot and its environment. It connects all of the tracks of this blog: geometry from 3D reconstruction (neural rendering), physics from simulators (post 3), predictions from world models (post 5), and display in XR.

  • Real-to-sim-to-real. RialTo (Torne et al. RSS 2024) builds a simulation of a real scene from a phone scan with a GUI, fine-tunes imitation policies with RL in that “digital twin”, and transfers them back, improving robustness.
  • Gaussian-splatting twins. SplatSim, RoboGSim and Real-is-Sim (2024 to 2025 preprints) render robots and objects inside 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructions for photoreal training and evaluation, narrowing the visual sim-to-real gap.
  • Mixed-reality robot interfaces. The VAM-HRI survey of Walker et al. (ACM THRI 2023) organizes how virtual, augmented and mixed reality are used in HRI, from showing robot intent to programming by demonstration in AR and remote supervision through a twin.
  • Egocentric digital twins. Aria Digital Twin shows the same idea for humans: a full 3D model of a space plus tracked people and objects, the kind of ground truth that world models and assistive robots both need.
flowchart TB
  S[Real scene] -->|scan: phone, Aria, robot cameras| G[3D reconstruction: meshes, 3DGS]
  G --> T[Digital twin: geometry + physics + semantics]
  R[Robot state] --> T
  T --> X[XR interface: supervise, teleoperate, program]
  T --> L[Policy training and evaluation]
  X -->|demonstrations, corrections| L
  L -->|policy| R

6. Research opportunities

This intersection is young and wide open. Directions that combine embodied AI, world models, AR/VR, HCI and graphics:

  1. XR-native data engines. Teleoperation interfaces designed with HCI methods for throughput and data quality, with real-time feedback on demonstration consistency, automatic segmentation and language annotation, and active requests for the demonstrations a policy needs most.
  2. Egocentric world models. Action-conditioned world models trained on head-mounted video (Aria, Vision Pro) that predict how the world responds to a person’s hands, usable both for AR assistance (“what happens if I pull this?”) and for robot planning.
  3. Closing the embodiment gap. Retargeting and representation learning that map human egocentric demonstrations to robot actions, including hand-object contact and force, with graphics-based hand-object reconstruction as supervision.
  4. Mixed-reality supervision of VLAs. Showing what a VLA “intends” (predicted chunks, attention, subgoals) in AR, letting people correct it in place, and using those corrections for online learning.
  5. Photoreal, physical digital twins. Fusing Gaussian splatting with simulation and generative world models, rendered efficiently (e.g. foveated) in headsets, for training, evaluation and remote operation.
  6. Haptics and multisensory feedback for dexterous teleoperation and for tactile datasets.
  7. Human-centred evaluation. Benchmarks that measure not only success rate but legibility, workload, trust and comfort when people share space with learned robots.
  8. Characters and robots. Physics-based character animation (DeepMimic, adversarial motion priors) and humanoid control now share methods and data; avatars in VR and humanoids in the real world can be driven by the same motion models.

As a map, the eight directions above all start from embodied AI and differ in which other fields they pull in:

Try it

The home-page Lab has a Foveated Rendering demo: your cursor is the simulated gaze, the scene is ray-marched at full resolution only around it and at 1/2 and 1/4 resolution further out, as in eye-tracked headsets such as Apple Vision Pro and Meta Quest Pro. Imagine streaming a robot’s stereo cameras or a digital twin to an operator this way. The Gaussian World tab shows the 3DGS representation that photoreal digital twins are built from, and the Cloth · XPBD tab the kind of physics they need.

2025-2026 update (as of November 2026)

The XR and HCI venues of 2026 have mostly taken place: HRI 2026 (March, Edinburgh), IEEE VR 2026 (March, Daegu), CHI 2026 (April, Barcelona) and ISMAR 2026 (October, Bari). UIST 2026 runs in Detroit this week (2-5 November). On the robotics side, the biggest change is that egocentric human data became pre-training data for robot foundation models, with scaling results to back it up. How motion capture and retargeting work for animated characters, the graphics side of section 1, is covered in Animation and characters.

Egocentric data at scale

  • Project Aria Gen 2 (Meta, announced February 2025) is the second generation of the research glasses of section 2. It weighs about 75 g and has on-device SLAM, eye and hand tracking, and a heart-rate (PPG) sensor. The Aria Gen 2 Pilot Dataset (arXiv preprint, October 2025) shows what it records. Meta targeted availability to research partners for 2026.
  • EgoDex (Hoque et al., Apple, ICLR 2026) has 829 hours of egocentric video over 194 tabletop tasks. It was recorded on Apple Vision Pro, so every frame comes with tracked 3D hand and finger poses. The headset’s own tracking becomes the action label, which is the point of section 2 made at scale.
  • EgoScale (Zheng et al., NVIDIA, arXiv preprint, February 2026) pre-trains a dexterous policy on 20,854 hours of human egocentric video, then adapts it to a 22-DoF robot hand. It reports a log-linear relation between hours of human data and robot performance, the first clear scaling law of this kind. GR00T N1.7 uses this data (post 5).
  • Nymeria (Ma et al., 2024) has 300 hours from 264 participants with Aria glasses plus full-body motion capture and language. NymeriaPlus (arXiv preprint, March 2026) adds object boxes and reconstructions. HOT3D (Banerjee et al., CVPR 2025) provides more than 3.7M images of hand-object interaction with 3D poses, recorded with Aria and Quest 3.

From human video to robot actions

The problem of section 2, that people and robots have different bodies, has three 2025-2026 answers:

  1. Share the action space. EgoMimic (Kareer et al., arXiv preprint, October 2024) co-trains on Aria human data and robot data with aligned hand and gripper trajectories. Humanoid policy ~ human policy (Qiu et al., arXiv preprint, March 2025) defines one state-action space for humans and humanoids. EgoVLA (Yang et al., arXiv preprint, July 2025) pre-trains a VLA on human wrist and hand actions and retargets them to the robot by inverse kinematics (post 1).
  2. Edit the pixels. Phantom (Lepert et al., CoRL 2025) inpaints the human arm out of the video and renders a robot in its place. The policy is trained only on these edited human videos and runs on the real robot without any robot data. Masquerade (Lepert et al., arXiv preprint, August 2025) applies the same editing to in-the-wild videos.
  3. Distil from web video. ZeroMimic (Shi et al., ICRA 2025) learns six types of manipulation skills purely from EpicKitchens videos and deploys them on two robots.

XR teleoperation, second generation

  • TWIST2 (Ze et al., arXiv preprint, November 2025) drops the motion-capture suit of TWIST. A consumer VR headset plus a low-cost 2-DoF robot neck give the operator an egocentric stereo view, as in Open-TeleVision. The authors report about 100 whole-body demonstrations in 15 minutes, and both the system and the data are open. Underneath, a motion tracker of the kind described in post 2 turns human poses into robot motion.
  • ARCap (Chen et al., arXiv preprint, October 2024) and ARMADA (Nechyporenko et al., arXiv preprint, December 2024) close the loop of section 3 with AR. The demonstrator collects bare-hand or handheld demonstrations without a robot, while the headset overlays a virtual robot and warns, visually or with haptics, when a motion would exceed the robot’s limits. Every demonstration is then feasible by construction.
  • GR-3 (post 5) and SONIC (post 2) treat VR-collected human trajectories as a regular training modality, not only as teleoperation.

HRI in the age of LLMs

A systematic review of HRI research with large language models (Wang et al., arXiv preprint, February 2026, 86 papers) follows the PRISMA procedure to map how HRI research uses LLMs and how such studies are designed and evaluated. It is a good companion to section 4. For 2026 papers at CHI, UIST and IEEE VR on immersive robot teleoperation, we could not verify a specific list in time for this update. The proceedings of those venues (ACM DL, IEEE Xplore) are the place to look.

What changed since the earlier sections: section 2 presented egocentric data as promising. By 2026 it is a main ingredient of commercial and open robot foundation models (GR00T N1.7, Being-H0.5, Helix 2.5’s human-behaviour pre-training), and the scaling evidence is in.

Representative papers

Paper Venue Year Link Why it matters

Loper et al., SMPL: a skinned multi-person linear model ACM TOG (SIGGRAPH Asia) 2015 DOI Standard body model

Yang et al., EgoVLA: learning vision-language-action models from egocentric human videos arXiv preprint (Jul 2025) 2025 arXiv VLA pre-trained on human hands
Lepert et al., Masquerade: learning from in-the-wild human videos using data-editing arXiv preprint (Aug 2025) 2025 arXiv Phantom-style editing at web scale

Meta, Introducing Aria Gen 2 blog 2025 see link Second-generation research glasses

Learning resources

  • Project Aria tools and datasets; Ego4D.
  • SMPL and MANO model pages; AMASS.
  • AnyTeleop project page; the Open-TeleVision and GELLO papers (linked in the table above) point to their open-source code.
  • The ACM/IEEE HRI conference and the VAM-HRI workshop series; ACM CHI and UIST for interaction techniques; IEEE VR and ISMAR for XR systems.
  • Graphics background for body models and skinning: the graphics track of this blog; for rendering in headsets, the foveated rendering demo on the home page.

Exercises

  1. Implement linear blend skinning for a 2-bone “arm” in 2-D (a strip of vertices, weights blending two joint transforms) and observe the “candy-wrapper” artefact when the elbow twists. How do SMPL’s pose-corrective blend shapes address it?
  2. Write a retargeting optimizer that maps a human shoulder-elbow-wrist trajectory (from any mocap clip) to the planar 3-link arm of post 1 using ik_dls with a smoothness term. Compare position-matching with direction-matching of links.
  3. Extend ClutchTeleop to rotation scaling (scale the axis-angle of $\Delta R$) and add a dead zone. Tune the 1€ filter’s min_cutoff and beta and plot jitter versus lag.
  4. Design a small user study for an XR teleoperation interface: two conditions (e.g. mono vs. stereo video), tasks, measures (success, time, NASA-TLX, demonstration smoothness) and the number of participants. What would you expect?

  5. Pick one of the research opportunities above and write a one-page proposal: the question, the system you would build, the data you would collect, and how you would evaluate it.

  6. Human-to-robot transfer (update section): for each of the three routes from human video to robot actions, say what must be estimated from the video and which error you expect to dominate on a parallel-jaw gripper.

    Hint

    Sharing the action space needs 3D wrist and hand trajectories in a frame aligned with the robot’s; errors in hand depth and the loss of finger degrees of freedom when mapping to a gripper dominate. Editing the pixels (Phantom, Masquerade) needs a hand-arm segmentation and pose good enough to inpaint the human and render the robot; rendering artefacts and pose errors dominate. Distilling from web video (ZeroMimic) must estimate where and how the hand grasps and the wrist motion afterwards, from uncalibrated footage; camera and scale ambiguity and imprecise grasp points dominate.

Where to go next: this is the last post of the embodied AI track. The world-models track explores the predictive models touched on here in depth, and the roadmap posts connect all tracks into one study plan.
entry.summary: Human motion capture and wearable sensing, egocentric data (Ego4D, Project Aria), VR/AR teleoperation for robot data collection, human-robot interaction, digital twins and mixed-reality interfaces, and research opportunities where embodied AI, world models, AR/VR, HCI and graphics meet.

entry.title: Vision-Language-Action models: RT-2, OpenVLA, pi0, GR00T and Gemini Robotics

link.title: Vision-Language-Action models: RT-2, OpenVLA, pi0, GR00T and Gemini Robotics

entry.content:
Why this matters

Imitation learning gives a robot one skill from a few dozen demonstrations. A Vision-Language-Action model (VLA) aims for a single policy that takes camera images and a natural-language instruction and outputs robot actions for many tasks, scenes and even robot bodies. The recipe borrows from large language and vision-language models: start from a model pre-trained on the internet, then train it on large, heterogeneous robot datasets such as Open X-Embodiment. Since 2023 this has become the main direction of robot learning in industry and academia. This post explains the main models, the design patterns that distinguish them, how they are evaluated, and where world models fit in.

Prerequisites

  • Posts 1 to 4, especially action chunking and diffusion/flow action heads (post 4).
  • Transformers and vision-language models (ViT/SigLIP encoders, LLM decoders, tokenization).
  • Flow matching or diffusion basics. The world-models track covers video world models and JEPA in depth.

1. From language-conditioned policies to VLAs

Early systems kept language and control separate. SayCan (Ahn et al. CoRL 2022) used an LLM to propose the next skill from a fixed library and multiplied the LLM’s score by a learned value function that estimated whether the skill could succeed in the current state, which grounded the language model in what the robot could actually do. The skills themselves were ordinary language-conditioned policies.

RT-1 (Brohan et al. RSS 2023) was the first large “Robotics Transformer”: a policy trained on about 130k real-world episodes covering over 700 tasks, collected with a fleet of 13 mobile manipulators over 17 months. It tokenizes images with a FiLM-conditioned EfficientNet (conditioned on the instruction embedding), compresses them with TokenLearner, and outputs discretized actions (256 bins per dimension for arm, base and mode) with a transformer at about 3 Hz. RT-1 showed that data scale and diversity, not clever algorithms, dominate generalization.

PaLM-E (Driess et al. ICML 2023) went the other way: inject continuous sensor observations (images, state estimates) as tokens into a large language model and train it end-to-end for embodied reasoning and planning. The largest version had 562B parameters and kept its general language abilities while learning robot planning tasks.

RT-2 (Brohan et al. CoRL 2023) merged the two ideas and coined the term VLA. It fine-tunes large vision-language models (PaLI-X and PaLM-E) to output robot actions as text tokens: each of the 7 action dimensions plus a termination flag is discretized into 256 bins and written as a string of integers. Crucially, it is co-fine-tuned on robot data and the original web vision-language data, so the model keeps its semantic knowledge. RT-2 could follow instructions involving concepts never seen in robot data (“move the banana to the sum of two plus one”, “pick up the extinct animal”) because that knowledge came from the web.

2. Open generalist policies

Model Year Backbone Action output Data Notes
Octo 2024 transformer trained from scratch (27M / 93M) diffusion head, action chunks 800k OXE trajectories flexible observation and goal tokens, easy fine-tuning
OpenVLA 2024 Llama 2 7B + DINOv2 + SigLIP (Prismatic VLM) 256-bin action tokens 970k OXE episodes open weights; beat RT-2-X (55B) by 16.5% absolute on 29 tasks
RDT-1B 2024 diffusion transformer, 1.2B diffusion over a unified action space multi-robot, bimanual focus “physically interpretable unified action space”
pi0 2024 PaliGemma 3B + 300M action expert flow matching, chunks of 50 large cross-embodiment mixture + OXE dexterous long-horizon tasks (laundry folding)
pi0.5 2025 pi0 lineage discrete (FAST) + flow-matching expert robot + web + high-level subtask data cleans kitchens and bedrooms in unseen homes
GR00T N1 2025 Eagle-2 VLM (System 2) + diffusion transformer (System 1) flow matching at high rate real + synthetic + human video “data pyramid” open model for humanoids
Gemini Robotics 2025 Gemini 2.0 low-latency action decoder large ALOHA 2 bimanual dataset + web plus Gemini Robotics-ER for embodied reasoning
SmolVLA 2025 small VLM (about 0.45B total) flow-matching action expert community LeRobot datasets runs on consumer hardware

Placed on a time line, the models of this post and the world-model work of section 5 show how quickly the field has moved since 2022:

Octo

Octo (Octo Model Team, RSS 2024) is a transformer-based policy pre-trained on 800k trajectories from Open X-Embodiment. Observations (several cameras, proprioception) and task specifications (language or goal images) are tokenized and processed by a transformer with block-wise attention; readout tokens feed a small diffusion head that predicts an action chunk. Its design goal is adaptability: new sensors or action spaces can be added during fine-tuning by adding tokenizers and heads.

OpenVLA

OpenVLA (Kim et al. CoRL 2024) is the open-source RT-2 analogue: a 7B Prismatic VLM (Llama 2 with fused DINOv2 and SigLIP features) fine-tuned on 970k episodes to output 256-bin action tokens, which overwrite the 256 least-used tokens of the Llama vocabulary. It showed that LoRA fine-tuning to new robots works on a single GPU and that the fused DINOv2+SigLIP vision encoder helps spatial reasoning. OpenVLA-OFT (Kim et al. RSS 2025) later found that an “optimized fine-tuning” recipe (parallel decoding of action chunks, continuous actions with an L1 loss) improves both success rate and inference speed considerably.

pi0 and pi0.5

pi0 (Black et al., Physical Intelligence, RSS 2025) adds a separate action expert (about 300M parameters) to a PaliGemma VLM. Images and language go through the VLM; the action expert processes proprioception and noisy action tokens, attends to the VLM’s tokens, and is trained with flow matching to output chunks of $H = 50$ continuous actions, which enables high-frequency dexterous control (laundry folding, table bussing, box assembly). The two sets of weights form a mixture-of-experts-like transformer: VLM tokens never attend to action tokens, so the VLM’s knowledge is protected.

FAST (Pertsch et al. RSS 2025) revisits discrete tokens: it compresses an action chunk with the discrete cosine transform, quantizes the coefficients and applies byte-pair encoding. Smooth chunks become a few tokens, which makes autoregressive VLAs trainable on high-frequency data and much faster to train than diffusion-style heads.

pi0.5 (Physical Intelligence, CoRL 2025) targets open-world generalization: a mobile manipulator cleaning kitchens and bedrooms in homes not seen during training. Its key ingredient is co-training on heterogeneous data: data from many robots, web data (captioning, VQA, object detection), and high-level semantic labels. At inference the model first predicts a high-level subtask in text (“pick up the plate”) and then the low-level actions for it, in one model. The authors report that performance in new homes rises with the number of distinct training environments.

GR00T N1

NVIDIA’s GR00T N1 (2025) is an open foundation model for humanoids with a dual-system architecture inspired by “thinking fast and slow”: System 2, a vision-language module (Eagle-2 VLM), interprets the scene and instruction at around 10 Hz, and System 1, a diffusion transformer trained with flow matching, generates motor actions at a high rate (the paper reports 120 Hz). The two are trained jointly end to end. Training uses a data pyramid: web and human video at the bottom, synthetic data from simulation and neural video generation in the middle, and real robot data at the top. Human videos and generated videos have no action labels, so latent actions or inverse-dynamics pseudo-labels are inferred for them.

Gemini Robotics

Google DeepMind’s Gemini Robotics (2025) builds a VLA on Gemini 2.0. A companion model, Gemini Robotics-ER (embodied reasoning), extends Gemini’s spatial understanding with pointing, object detection, 3D bounding boxes, trajectory and grasp prediction. The VLA itself splits into a backbone in the cloud and a local action decoder to keep latency low, and the report shows long-horizon dexterous tasks on ALOHA 2, fast adaptation to new short tasks from around 100 demonstrations, and adaptation to new robot bodies. Gemini Robotics 1.5 (technical report, 2025) adds “thinking” before acting and transfers motions learned on one embodiment to others.

3. Design patterns

flowchart LR
  I[Camera images] --> V[Vision encoder: SigLIP / DINOv2]
  L[Language instruction] --> T[Tokenizer]
  V --> B[VLM backbone, pre-trained on web data]
  T --> B
  P[Proprioception] --> E
  B -->|tokens or KV cache| E[Action head]
  E --> A[Action chunk a_t ... a_t+H]
  A --> C[Low-level controller: IK, impedance, PD]

The two dominant ways to attach actions to a VLM, drawn side by side:

Action representation

Two families dominate:

  1. Discrete action tokens (RT-1, RT-2, OpenVLA, FAST). Each dimension $a^{(j)}\in[\ell_j, u_j]$ is mapped to a bin $b^{(j)} = \lfloor (a^{(j)}-\ell_j)/(u_j-\ell_j)\cdot 256\rfloor$, and the model is trained with the usual next-token cross-entropy. Pros: reuses the LLM machinery unchanged; categorical outputs are naturally multimodal. Cons: one token per dimension per step makes high-frequency chunks long and slow to decode, unless compressed (FAST).
  2. Continuous generative heads (Octo, pi0, GR00T, RDT): a diffusion or flow-matching model predicts a whole chunk conditioned on backbone features. Pros: precise, smooth, fast for long chunks with a few integration steps. Cons: an extra network, and gradients from the action loss can disturb the pre-trained backbone (later work from Physical Intelligence on “knowledge insulation” stops those gradients and trains the backbone on discrete tokens instead).

Both rely on action chunking (post 4) and on careful normalization (per-dataset quantiles, e.g. mapping the 1st and 99th percentiles to $\pm 1$), because robots and datasets differ in units and ranges.

The code below shows both: 256-bin tokenization with its quantization error, and DCT compression in the spirit of FAST.

import numpy as np
from scipy.fft import dct, idct

# ---- RT-2 / OpenVLA style: 256 uniform bins per action dimension ----
def to_bins(a, low, high, n_bins=256):
    a = np.clip(a, low, high)
    return np.minimum(((a - low) / (high - low) * n_bins).astype(int), n_bins - 1)

def from_bins(b, low, high, n_bins=256):
    return low + (b + 0.5) * (high - low) / n_bins        # bin centers

# a smooth 7-D action chunk (xyz, rpy, gripper) at 50 Hz for 1 s
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 50)[:, None]
chunk = np.concatenate([0.05 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t * [1, 0.5, 0.25]),
                        0.1 * np.cos(np.pi * t * [1, 2, 3]),
                        (t > 0.5).astype(float)], axis=1)  # [50, 7]
low, high = chunk.min(0) - 1e-3, chunk.max(0) + 1e-3     # per-dimension range (from the dataset)
tokens = to_bins(chunk, low, high)                        # [50, 7] integers -> 350 tokens
err = np.abs(from_bins(tokens, low, high) - chunk).max()
print(f"binning: {tokens.size} tokens, max error {err:.5f}")

# ---- FAST-style: DCT along time, quantize, keep the few non-zero coefficients ----
coef = dct(chunk, axis=0, norm="ortho")                   # [50, 7] frequency coefficients
for scale in [10.0, 50.0, 200.0]:
    q = np.round(coef * scale).astype(int)                # most high frequencies round to 0
    recon = idct(q / scale, axis=0, norm="ortho")
    print(f"DCT scale {scale:5.0f}: {np.count_nonzero(q):3d} non-zero of {q.size} coefficients, "
          f"mean error {np.abs(recon - chunk).mean():.4f}")

binning: 350 tokens, max error 0.00096
DCT scale    10:  35 non-zero of 350 coefficients, mean error 0.0052
DCT scale    50:  42 non-zero of 350 coefficients, mean error 0.0016
DCT scale   200:  57 non-zero of 350 coefficients, mean error 0.0005

A one-second chunk at 50 Hz costs 350 tokens with per-step binning, but only a few dozen non-zero DCT coefficients, because smooth motions concentrate their energy in low frequencies. FAST then run-length/BPE-encodes the sparse integer matrix into a short token sequence; the scale is the knob between compression and precision.

The figures below show what these numbers mean for the chunk built in the code: first the 256-bin grid on one dimension, then where the DCT puts the chunk’s energy.

A flow-matching action expert

The other family, in the style of pi0 and GR00T, learns a velocity field that transports Gaussian noise to the action chunk, conditioned on the backbone’s features $c$. With the linear path $A^t = (1-t)\,\epsilon + t\,A$, the target velocity is constant, $\frac{d}{dt}A^t = A - \epsilon$, and the loss is

\[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t\sim p(t),\,\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I),\,(A,c)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\left\lVert v_\theta(A^t, t, c) - (A - \epsilon)\right\rVert^2\right].\]

Sampling integrates $dA/dt = v_\theta$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 1$, typically with about 10 Euler steps. (pi0 uses the same idea with its own time convention and a Beta-shaped distribution $p(t)$ that emphasizes the noisier time steps.) In the toy below, a random vector stands in for the VLM embedding of two instructions, “go left” and “go right”:

import math
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
H, A, C = 8, 2, 64           # chunk length, action dim, size of the "VLM" context embedding

class ActionExpert(nn.Module):
    """v_theta(A_t, t, c): predicts the flow velocity for a whole action chunk.
    pi0 uses a transformer "action expert" attending to the VLM's tokens; an MLP keeps this toy fast."""
    def __init__(self, hidden=256):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(H * A + C + 32, hidden), nn.SiLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.SiLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.SiLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(hidden, H * A))
    def forward(self, a_t, t, c):
        freqs = torch.exp(torch.arange(16) * (-math.log(1000.0) / 16))
        emb = 1000 * t[:, None] * freqs[None]             # sinusoidal embedding of flow time
        x = torch.cat([a_t.flatten(1), c, emb.sin(), emb.cos()], -1)
        return self.net(x).view(-1, H, A)

def flow_matching_loss(model, actions, ctx):
    """Linear path from noise (t=0) to data (t=1); regress the constant velocity."""
    eps = torch.randn_like(actions)
    t = torch.rand(actions.shape[0])
    a_t = (1 - t)[:, None, None] * eps + t[:, None, None] * actions
    return F.mse_loss(model(a_t, t, ctx), actions - eps)

@torch.no_grad()
def sample(model, ctx, steps=10):
    a = torch.randn(ctx.shape[0], H, A)
    for i in range(steps):                                # forward Euler on da/dt = v
        t = torch.full((ctx.shape[0],), i / steps)
        a = a + model(a, t, ctx) / steps
    return a

# toy data: two instructions ("go left" / "go right") encoded as fixed context vectors
instr = torch.randn(2, C)
def batch(n):
    side = torch.randint(0, 2, (n,))
    tt = torch.linspace(0, 1, H)
    y = (side.float() * 2 - 1)[:, None] * torch.sin(math.pi * tt) * 0.5
    return torch.stack([tt.expand(n, H), y], -1), instr[side], side

model = ActionExpert()
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
for it in range(3000):
    act, ctx, _ = batch(128)
    loss = flow_matching_loss(model, act, ctx)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
act, ctx, side = batch(512)
pred = sample(model, ctx)
ok = (torch.sign(pred[:, H // 2, 1]) == (side * 2 - 1)).float().mean()
print(f"final loss {loss.item():.4f}; follows the instruction in {ok:.1%} of samples; "
      f"chunk error {(pred - act).abs().mean():.3f}")

final loss 0.0246; follows the instruction in 100.0% of samples; chunk error 0.018

Ten Euler steps of a small network turn noise into the right chunk for each instruction. In a real VLA the context is the backbone’s tokens (attended to by a transformer action expert), the chunk has 50 steps and 7 to 30+ dimensions, and the instruction set is open-ended.

Recording the ten Euler steps shows the flow at work: noise chunks are transported, in straight lines on average, to the chunk that matches each instruction.

Cross-embodiment training

Datasets differ in robots, cameras, control frequencies and action spaces. Common choices:

  • A shared action convention, usually end-effector deltas plus gripper, normalized per dataset; or a padded “unified” action vector where each embodiment fills its own slots (RDT, pi0), plus an embodiment or dataset token.
  • Data mixtures with weights: heavily used datasets are down-weighted, diverse ones up-weighted; pi0.5 shows that web and cross-robot data improve generalization in new environments even for a single target robot.
  • Human and synthetic data without actions (GR00T’s data pyramid): latent action models infer pseudo-actions from consecutive frames, so video can teach motion priors.

Hierarchy and reasoning

Long tasks need planning. Options range from an external LLM/VLM planner calling a VLA (SayCan style), to a single model that predicts subtasks before actions (pi0.5), to dual-system designs with a slow reasoner and a fast actor (GR00T N1, Figure’s Helix as described in its public announcement), and “embodied chain-of-thought” that reasons in text or with pointing and boxes before acting (Gemini Robotics-ER and 1.5).

4. Scaling and evaluation

Evaluating VLAs is hard: each real rollout costs minutes of human time, success depends on the scene setup, and variance across seeds and evaluators is large. Practices that have emerged:

  • Generalization axes: visual (new backgrounds, lighting, distractors), semantic (new objects, new instructions), behavioural (new positions, new motions), and embodiment (new robots). RT-2 and OpenVLA report results along these axes.
  • Standardized simulated proxies: LIBERO for fine-tuning comparisons, SimplerEnv (post 3) for policies trained on real Google-robot and WidowX data, with explicit measurement of sim-real correlation.
  • Blind A/B evaluations across institutions and pairwise comparisons, which reduce evaluator bias.
  • Scaling studies: pi0.5’s environment-count scaling, OXE’s cross-embodiment gains, and GR00T’s mixtures suggest that diversity of scenes and embodiments matters at least as much as raw episode count. Unlike language models, we do not yet have clean power laws for robot success rate.

Deployment concerns are very practical: inference latency (a 7B model at a few Hz needs chunking and asynchronous execution), on-robot compute, safety constraints in the low-level controller, and failure detection.

5. World models for robot learning

A world model predicts how observations evolve given actions. The world-models track discusses them in depth; here are the main ways they meet robotics:

  1. Learned simulators for RL. Dreamer-style agents learn a latent dynamics model and train the policy in imagination. DayDreamer (Wu et al. CoRL 2022) trained a quadruped to walk from scratch in about an hour of real-world interaction, and DreamerV3 (Hafner et al., Nature 2025) generalized the recipe across domains.
  2. Video prediction as planning. UniPi (Du et al. NeurIPS 2023) generates a video of the task being done from a text instruction, then extracts actions with an inverse dynamics model. GR-1 (Wu et al. ICLR 2024) pre-trains a GPT-style model on large-scale video prediction and fine-tunes it to predict actions and future frames jointly.
  3. Interactive simulators from video. UniSim (Yang et al. ICLR 2024) learns an action-conditioned video simulator from diverse data and uses it to train policies and planners; Genie (Bruce et al. ICML 2024) learns latent actions from unlabeled video so the resulting world can be controlled. NVIDIA’s Cosmos world foundation models (2025) are designed to be post-trained into robot- and driving-specific simulators and synthetic data generators (GR00T’s “neural trajectories” are one use).
  4. Latent planning. V-JEPA 2 (Assran et al., 2025) pre-trains a video encoder with a joint-embedding predictive objective on over a million hours of internet video, then trains an action-conditioned predictor (V-JEPA 2-AC) on about 62 hours of unlabeled robot video from DROID. Planning with goal images in the learned latent space enabled zero-shot pick-and-place on Franka arms in two labs, with no task-specific data or rewards.
  5. Policy evaluation. Because real evaluation is expensive, an action-conditioned world model can serve as a learned evaluator that ranks policies before they reach the robot, provided it is validated against real outcomes.
flowchart TB
  D[Robot and human video] --> W[World model]
  W --> R1[Imagined rollouts for RL]
  W --> R2[Synthetic demonstrations]
  W --> R3[Latent planning / MPC]
  W --> R4[Policy evaluation]
  R1 --> P[Policy / VLA]
  R2 --> P
  R3 --> P

The open question is whether one model can be both: a VLA that predicts actions and a world model that predicts their consequences, trained jointly so each improves the other. Several 2025 systems already train action and future-frame prediction together.

6. Open problems

  • Data: robot data is still orders of magnitude smaller than text or video; human video, simulation and XR teleoperation (post 6) are the main levers.
  • Precision and contact: VLAs are good at semantics and coarse motion, weaker at millimetre-precise, force-sensitive manipulation; tactile sensing and force-aware action spaces are active areas.
  • Memory and long horizons: most VLAs see only the last frame or two.
  • Reliability: 80% success is impressive in a paper and unacceptable in a home; learning from deployment (RL fine-tuning, interventions) is the next frontier.
  • Evaluation that is reproducible across labs.

Try it

The home-page Lab has a “Gaussian World” demo: describe a world and an editable open world of about 200,000 3D Gaussians is built (a keyword-driven procedural generator stands in for a learned model) and stays live: relit, sculptable, walkable. It is a tiny analogue of the generative world models above. Combined with the XPBD physics demo, it hints at the long-term picture: generative 3D worlds with physics, in which VLAs are trained and evaluated.

2025-2026 update (as of November 2026)

The sections above describe the field as of early 2026. This section adds what appeared since, up to November 2026. ICLR 2026 (April, Rio de Janeiro), ICRA 2026 (June, Vienna), ICML 2026 (July) and RSS 2026 (July, Sydney) have taken place. CoRL 2026 (9-12 November, Austin) is a week away, so its papers are cited here as preprints. For every work the status is given as published, accepted, preprint or announcement. Many industrial models have only a blog post, and we say so.

The explorer below places the models of this post and of this update on one time line. Each lane is a lab or family, and each grey curve means “builds on”. Use the filters to see three trends: flow matching taking over action heads, open weights spreading from academia to NVIDIA and Physical Intelligence, and humanoids becoming a main target in 2026.

Interactive: filter by action head, open weights or embodiment. Tap or click a model to see its summary, status and link (summaries are in English). Colour = action head; a filled marker = open weights; grey curves = builds on. On a phone the time axis runs downwards and long names are shortened; tap an entry for the full name. Dates are the first arXiv version or the official announcement.

Physical Intelligence: from pi0.5 to pi0.7

  • Knowledge insulation (Driess et al., NeurIPS 2025) fixes a problem with adding an action expert to a VLM: its gradients can damage the VLM’s knowledge. The backbone is trained on discrete FAST tokens and web data, while the flow-matching expert reads the backbone’s features through a stop-gradient. Training stays fast, inference keeps continuous chunks, and language following improves. The openpi pi0.5 checkpoints use this recipe.
  • Real-time chunking (Black et al., NeurIPS 2025) runs chunked flow policies asynchronously. While the robot executes the current chunk, the next one is generated as an inpainting problem: the actions already committed are frozen and the overlap is guided toward them. No retraining is needed. It removes the pauses and jerks at chunk boundaries described in section 3.
  • pi*0.6 (Physical Intelligence, arXiv preprint, November 2025) introduces Recap (RL with experience and corrections via advantage-conditioned policies). A value function scores every segment of demonstrations, expert corrections and autonomous rollouts. The VLA is then trained conditioned on a binarized advantage, and at deployment it is asked for “good” actions. This is offline RL without policy gradients through the flow head. The company reports more than doubled throughput on its hardest tasks (espresso making, folding laundry in homes, box assembly). Post 2 explains advantages.
  • pi0.7 (arXiv preprint, April 2026) makes the prompt richer. Besides language, it carries episode metadata (demonstration quality and speed), the control modality and optional subgoal images. Data of mixed quality, and data from other embodiments, can then be used without spoiling the policy: at test time the prompt asks for “high-quality”. The report shows zero-shot laundry folding on an embodiment without folding data. Two research posts on pi.website (March 2026), not peer-reviewed, add memory (compressed video plus text notes for tasks of about 15 minutes) and an “RL token” for fast online RL. The RL token later appeared as an arXiv preprint (post 2).

Google DeepMind: Gemini Robotics 1.5 to 2

Gemini Robotics On-Device (June 2025, announcement) was the first DeepMind VLA that runs without a network and can be fine-tuned with 50-100 demonstrations. Gemini Robotics-ER 1.6 (April 2026, available through the Gemini API) improves pointing, counting and success detection, and adds gauge reading developed with Boston Dynamics. Gemini Robotics 2 (July 2026 announcement; VLA for early-access partners, ER 2 as a preview) extends control from bimanual tabletop work to whole-body humanoids such as Apptronik’s Apollo 2. In the GR 2 family, ER 2 coordinates several robots on multi-minute tasks, and On-Device 2 adapts to a new bi-arm body with fewer than 200 examples. None of these has a full paper, only blog posts and a safety report, so architecture claims beyond the announcements are unknown.

NVIDIA: GR00T N1.5 to N1.7, and N2 as a world action model

  • GR00T N1.5 (June 2025, open weights) freezes the Eagle 2.5 VLM and adds FLARE, a loss that aligns the policy’s features with embeddings of future observations. It also trains on DreamGen “neural trajectories” (below).
  • GR00T N1.6 (December 2025, open weights under a non-commercial licence) switches to a Cosmos-based 2B VLM with its top layers unfrozen and a 32-layer action DiT. It predicts state-relative action chunks, an instance of the normalization question of section 3.
  • GR00T N1.7 (March 2026 early access, now on GitHub) uses a Cosmos-Reason2-2B backbone. It adds about 20k hours of egocentric human video from EgoScale (post 6) through a relative end-effector action space shared by human hands and robot grippers.
  • DreamZero (Ye et al., arXiv preprint, February 2026) argues that world action models are zero-shot policies. A 14B autoregressive video-diffusion model generates the future video and the actions together, and runs closed loop at about 7 Hz. NVIDIA previewed GR00T N2 on this design at GTC in March 2026 for release “by the end of the year”. As of November 2026 it is announced but not released.

Figure: Helix, Helix 02 and Helix 2.5

Helix (February 2025, announcement) is the dual-system design mentioned in section 3: a 7B VLM (System 2) at 7-9 Hz passes a latent vector to an 80M-parameter transformer (System 1) that controls the 35-DoF upper body at 200 Hz, entirely on board. Helix 02 (January 2026) adds System 0, a learned whole-body controller at 1 kHz trained on retargeted human motion. This is the motion-tracking RL of post 2, now inside a VLA stack. Helix 2.5 (September 2026) reports zero-shot operation in 30 unseen homes after pre-training on human behaviour data. These are company announcements without papers or open evaluation.

Open models from academia and other companies

  • UniVLA (Bu et al., RSS 2025) learns task-centric latent actions from video in DINO feature space, so internet and human video become pre-training data. A small decoder maps latent actions to each robot.
  • X-VLA (Zheng et al., ICLR 2026) handles cross-embodiment data with soft prompts: one learnable embedding per data source, prepended to the tokens. With a plain 0.9B transformer and a flow-matching head, the per-source embedding absorbs camera and action-space differences (compare the unified action vector figure above).
  • GR-3 (ByteDance Seed, technical report, July 2025) is about 4B parameters (a Qwen2.5-VL backbone and a flow-matching DiT). It is co-trained on web data, VR-collected human trajectories and robot data for a bimanual mobile robot.
  • WALL-OSS (X Square Robot, arXiv preprint, September 2025) links instruction reasoning, subgoals and actions in a “unified cross-level chain of thought”. It was released in flow and FAST variants.
  • RDT2 (Liu et al., ICML 2026) trains a 7B VLM on more than 10k hours of UMI handheld-gripper data (post 4), with RVQ-token and flow-matching variants. It is deployed zero-shot on robots that were never in the training set. Because the gripper is the shared “embodiment”, the robot arm becomes almost interchangeable.
  • MolmoAct2 (Fang et al., Ai2, arXiv preprint, May 2026) is fully open: weights, code, a 720-hour bimanual dataset and an open FAST-style tokenizer. Its flow-matching expert reads the backbone’s per-layer key-value cache.
  • OAT, ordered action tokenization (Liu et al., RSS 2026, outstanding-paper finalist) designs action tokens whose prefixes can already be decoded into coarse actions, a step beyond FAST’s DCT ordering.

World action models: predicting video and actions together

Section 5 asked whether one model can be both policy and world model. In 2025-2026 several groups built such models:

  • WorldVLA (Cen et al., arXiv preprint, June 2025) and Unified VLA (Wang et al., ICLR 2026) put image, language and action tokens into one autoregressive model. Unified VLA is post-trained as a world model on video.
  • Genie Envisioner (Liao et al., arXiv preprint, August 2025) trains a video-diffusion world model (GE-Base), a flow-matching action decoder on its latents (GE-Act), and a neural simulator (GE-Sim).
  • DreamGen (Jang et al., CoRL 2025) uses a fine-tuned video model as a data generator. It “dreams” videos of new behaviours, labels them with inverse dynamics, and trains GR00T on these neural trajectories, reaching 22 new behaviours from teleoperation data of a single task.
  • Cosmos Policy (Kim et al., ICLR 2026) fine-tunes the Cosmos-Predict2 video model so that actions, future states and values are encoded as extra latent frames. One network is then policy, world model and value function, and can plan by best-of-N sampling.
  • DreamZero / GR00T N2 (above) is the largest so far.

The common pattern: a video-generative backbone replaces the VLM backbone, and actions become one more modality to denoise. The bet is that video pre-training teaches physics and motion better than captions do. The cost is inference speed (a few Hz rather than tens of Hz). The world-models track (video world simulators) covers the video models themselves. How engines and these models are converging into data factories is the subject of AI meets graphics engines.

RL fine-tuning of VLAs

Besides Recap, open work applies policy-gradient RL to pre-trained VLAs in simulation. RL4VLA (Liu et al., NeurIPS 2025) finds that PPO fine-tuning improves semantic and execution generalization over supervised fine-tuning, and that PPO beats DPO and GRPO there. SimpleVLA-RL (Li et al., arXiv preprint, September 2025) scales outcome-reward RL on OpenVLA-OFT with the veRL framework and reduces the demonstrations needed. Post 2 covers flow-policy RL (pi_RL) and real-world variants.

Evaluation

  • RoboArena (Atreya et al., CoRL 2025) crowd-sources real-world evaluation. Policies run on DROID-style Franka setups at many institutions, evaluators compare two anonymous policies on a task they choose, and a pairwise-preference model turns the votes into a ranking. This is the blind A/B idea of section 4 at scale.
  • RoboChallenge (Yakefu et al., arXiv preprint, October 2025) is a hosted remote benchmark: teams submit policies that run on real robots for a fixed set of 30 tasks (Table30).
  • World models as evaluators: Google DeepMind evaluates Gemini Robotics policies in a fine-tuned Veo world simulator, including safety probes, and checks the results against real trials (arXiv preprint, December 2025). This is item 5 of section 5 in practice. Post 3 has more.

What changed since the earlier sections: the summary table of section 2 now has successors for almost every row. The claim in section 4 that robot learning has no clean scaling laws still holds for success rates, but EgoScale (post 6) reports a log-linear relation between hours of human-video pre-training and downstream dexterous performance.

Representative papers
