Industry announcements: Helix, Helix 02, Gemini Robotics On-Device, Gemini Robotics 2, GR00T N1.5, GR00T N1.6 announcement 2025-2026 see links No papers; official pages only

Learning resources

  • OpenVLA code and openpi (open pi0 / pi0.5 weights and fine-tuning code).
  • LeRobot: pi0, SmolVLA, ACT and Diffusion Policy in one library.
  • Octo and Isaac GR00T.
  • Open X-Embodiment datasets in RLDS format.
  • Surveys and courses: Stanford CS 224R (deep RL and robot learning), CMU 16-831, and the robotics chapters of Tedrake’s Robotic Manipulation.

Exercises

  1. Compute how many tokens RT-2-style binning needs for a 2-second chunk at 50 Hz with 14 dimensions (a bimanual robot), and compare with FAST at the three scales above.
  2. Change the flow-matching toy so the context contains noise (the two instructions are only partially separable). How does the instruction-following rate change? Then sample with 1, 2, 5 and 10 Euler steps.
  3. Replace the MLP action expert with a small transformer that attends to a sequence of 16 “VLM tokens” instead of a single vector. What changes in training speed and accuracy?
  4. Read the OpenVLA and pi0 papers and draw both architectures in the same diagram style as the Mermaid figure above. Mark which weights are pre-trained, which are trained from scratch, and where gradients flow.
  5. Design an evaluation protocol for a VLA in your lab: list the generalization axes, the number of trials per condition, and how you would estimate confidence intervals for success rates.

  6. In the VLA explorer, select Flow and Open weights only. How many open flow-matching models does the list contain per year, and which earlier model do most of the “builds on” curves of the 2025 ones lead back to?

    Hint

    One in 2024 (pi0), seven in 2025 (pi0.5, GR00T N1, N1.5, N1.6, SmolVLA, WALL-OSS, X-VLA) and three in 2026 (N1.7, RDT2, MolmoAct2). Within this list the open flow models of 2025 trace back mostly to pi0 or to the GR00T line; several (X-VLA, WALL-OSS) have no recorded parent, which only means that the list does not record one. Remember that the list is a curated selection.

Next: Embodied AI meets XR and HCI, where humans, headsets and robots meet.
entry.summary: How robot foundation models are built: from RT-1 and RT-2 to Octo, OpenVLA, pi0/pi0.5, GR00T N1 and Gemini Robotics; action tokenization versus flow-matching heads, cross-embodiment training, evaluation, and how world models enter robot learning.

entry.title: Imitation learning: behavior cloning, DAgger, ACT and Diffusion Policy

link.title: Imitation learning: behavior cloning, DAgger, ACT and Diffusion Policy

entry.content:
Why this matters

RL (post 2) needs a reward and a lot of trials, which is fine for walking in a GPU simulator and painful for folding a shirt or plugging in a cable. Imitation learning (IL) skips the reward: a human demonstrates the task, and the robot learns a policy that maps observations to the demonstrated actions. Since 2023, two ideas, action chunking and generative action models (diffusion and flow matching), made IL work for fine-grained, contact-rich manipulation from a few dozen demonstrations. They are also the action heads of today’s Vision-Language-Action models (post 5). This post builds IL from the ground up and ends with a working Diffusion Policy training loop. The simulators of the previous post are where you can practice it before touching a robot.

Prerequisites

  • Supervised learning with PyTorch; the RL notation of post 2 ($\pi$, trajectories, horizon $T$).
  • Diffusion models at the level of DDPM (forward noising, noise prediction). The world-models and neural-rendering tracks cover these too.
  • The action-space discussion of post 1 (joint vs. end-effector targets, impedance control).

1. Behavior cloning and covariate shift

Given demonstrations $\mathcal{D} = \lbrace(o_i, a_i)\rbrace$ from an expert policy $\pi^{\ast}$, behavior cloning (BC) fits a policy by maximum likelihood:

\[\theta^{\ast} = \arg\max_\theta \sum_{(o,a)\in\mathcal{D}} \log \pi_\theta(a \mid o).\]

With a fixed-variance Gaussian policy this is just MSE regression. BC is the oldest robot learning method (ALVINN drove a vehicle from camera images with a small neural network in 1988) and it is still the backbone of most manipulation systems. It has two classic failure modes.

Covariate shift and compounding errors

BC trains on states from the expert’s distribution $d_{\pi^{\ast}}$, but at test time the robot visits states from its own distribution $d_{\pi_\theta}$. A small mistake moves it to a state no demonstration covers, where it makes a bigger mistake, and so on. Ross and Bagnell (2010) formalized this: if the learned policy errs with probability $\epsilon$ on the expert’s states, the expected cost over a horizon $T$ can grow as $O(\epsilon T^2)$, while a learner trained on its own state distribution achieves $O(\epsilon T)$.

A small experiment makes the effect visible. A point moves forward at constant speed and steers its lateral position $y$ to follow a sine-shaped path; the expert is a simple feedback law, and the learner is a radial-basis-function regressor fitted to the expert’s state-action pairs:

DAgger

DAgger (Dataset Aggregation; Ross, Gordon and Bagnell, AISTATS 2011) fixes the distribution mismatch by querying the expert on states the learner visits:

  1. Train $\pi_1$ on the expert demonstrations $\mathcal{D}$.
  2. For $i = 1, 2, \dots$: run $\pi_i$ (optionally mixed with the expert) to collect states; ask the expert to label them with $a = \pi^{\ast}(s)$; aggregate $\mathcal{D} \leftarrow \mathcal{D} \cup \lbrace(s, \pi^{\ast}(s))\rbrace$; retrain $\pi_{i+1}$.

DAgger has no-regret guarantees and the $O(\epsilon T)$ bound, but labelling arbitrary states is awkward for a human teleoperator. Practical variants let the human intervene only when the robot goes wrong (HG-DAgger, intervention data in many real systems), or use a privileged simulator policy as the expert, which is exactly the teacher-student distillation from post 2. Other remedies for covariate shift: inject noise during demonstrations so the data contains recoveries (DART), augment observations, and, most effectively in practice, predict action chunks (section 2).

Multimodality

Humans solve the same task in different ways: go around an obstacle on the left or on the right, grasp a mug by the handle or the rim. The MSE-optimal prediction is the average of the modes, which may be the one action that fails (straight into the obstacle). Remedies are expressive action distributions: discretized actions with a categorical output (RT-1, post 5), Gaussian mixtures (robomimic’s BC-RNN-GMM), energy-based models (Implicit BC), k-means “action bins” plus offsets (Behavior Transformers), VAEs (ACT), and diffusion or flow models (Diffusion Policy). The code at the end of this post shows MSE BC collapsing onto the obstacle while a diffusion policy keeps both modes.

The figure shows this with the toy problem trained in section 6: demonstrations pass an obstacle on the left or on the right, and the MSE regressor averages the two.

2. Action chunking with transformers (ACT / ALOHA)

Zhao et al. (RSS 2023) built ALOHA, a low-cost bimanual teleoperation system in which a human moves two small “leader” arms and two “follower” arms mirror the joint positions, and ACT (Action Chunking with Transformers), which learned tasks like opening a translucent condiment cup and slotting a battery with 80 to 90% success from about 10 minutes of demonstrations. The key ideas:

  • Action chunking. Instead of one action per step, predict the next $k$ actions $a_{t:t+k}$ (e.g. $k = 100$ joint targets at 50 Hz). Chunking reduces the effective horizon by a factor of $k$, so compounding errors have fewer opportunities to accumulate, and it lets the model represent temporally correlated behaviour such as pauses, which single-step policies handle poorly.
  • Temporal ensembling. Querying the policy every step yields overlapping chunks. ACT averages all predictions for the current time step with exponential weights $w_i = \exp(-m\, i)$, where $i = 0$ is the oldest prediction, which smooths motion without lag.
  • CVAE training. A transformer encoder compresses the demonstrated chunk into a latent style variable $z$; the decoder (a transformer over ResNet image features from several cameras and the joint state) predicts the chunk given $z$. At test time $z$ is set to the prior mean. The objective is reconstruction (L1) plus a KL term.
  • Joint-space actions with a position controller, which avoids IK and singularities for the 6-DoF ALOHA arms.

Mobile ALOHA (Fu et al. CoRL 2024) put the system on a mobile base and showed that co-training with the static ALOHA data improves mobile manipulation. ALOHA Unleashed (Zhao et al. CoRL 2024) scaled data collection and used a diffusion-based policy for tasks like tying shoelaces and hanging shirts.

Temporal ensembling is easiest to understand on a timeline. In the toy below, every chunk is the ideal action plus an error that grows along the chunk, as a learned policy’s would:

3. Diffusion Policy

Chi et al. (RSS 2023) model the conditional distribution of an action sequence with a denoising diffusion model. A policy step starts from Gaussian noise and iteratively denoises it into an action chunk, conditioned on recent observations. Across 12 tasks from 4 benchmarks it improved success rates by 46.9% on average over the prior state of the art.

Formulation

Let $A^0_t \in \mathbb{R}^{T_p\times d_a}$ be a chunk of $T_p$ future actions and $O_t$ the last $T_o$ observations. The DDPM forward process adds noise with a schedule $\bar\alpha_k$:

\[A^k_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}\,A^0_t + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\,\epsilon, \qquad \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0, I),\]

and the network $\epsilon_\theta$ learns to predict that noise:

\[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{k,\,\epsilon,\,(O_t, A^0_t)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\left\lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta\!\left(A^k_t,\, k,\, O_t\right)\right\rVert^2\right].\]

At inference, starting from $A^K_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, each reverse step is

\[A^{k-1}_t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_k}}\left(A^k_t - \frac{\beta_k}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}}\,\epsilon_\theta(A^k_t, k, O_t)\right) + \sigma_k z, \qquad z\sim\mathcal{N}(0, I),\]

with $\beta_k = 1-\alpha_k$ and $\sigma_k^2 = \beta_k$. Since $\epsilon_\theta$ is (up to scale) the score $\nabla_A \log p(A \mid O)$, sampling is noisy gradient ascent on the log-density of actions, which naturally represents multiple modes and high-dimensional, temporally coherent action sequences.

The forward process is easy to picture for an action chunk: each of its waypoints is shrunk toward the origin and blurred with Gaussian noise until nothing of the trajectory remains.

Design choices that matter

  • Receding horizon. Predict $T_p$ steps (e.g. 16), execute only the first $T_a$ (e.g. 8), then replan from new observations ($T_o = 2$ frames). Executing a chunk gives temporal consistency; replanning gives reactivity.
  • Conditioning, not joint modelling. Observations condition the denoiser (via FiLM layers in a 1-D temporal CNN U-Net, or cross-attention in a transformer variant) instead of being denoised, so the vision encoder runs once per policy step, not once per denoising step.
  • Position control in end-effector space worked better than velocity control in their experiments: absolute targets suffer less from compounding drift.
  • Fast sampling. Training uses 100 DDPM steps; inference can use DDIM with about 10 steps. Later work replaces diffusion with flow matching (pi0, post 5) or consistency distillation to reach real-time rates.

Extensions include 3D Diffusion Policy (Ze et al. RSS 2024), which conditions on point clouds, and the extended journal version (Chi et al. IJRR 2024).

4. Collecting demonstrations

The data is the real bottleneck. Common interfaces:

Interface Examples Pros Cons
Kinesthetic teaching pushing a compliant arm by hand intuitive, no extra hardware human in the camera view, single arm
Leader-follower arms ALOHA, GELLO low latency, bimanual, joint-space, force feel via backdrivability robot-specific hardware
VR / AR teleoperation Quest or Vision Pro hand tracking, Open-TeleVision immersive, dexterous hands, remote retargeting, latency, no haptics (post 6)
Space mouse / phone robomimic, RoboTurk cheap, scalable slow, hard for dexterous tasks
Hand-held grippers UMI no robot needed, in-the-wild data needs pose tracking and embodiment matching
Human video Ego4D, EgoMimic huge scale no actions, embodiment gap (post 6)

UMI (Universal Manipulation Interface; Chi et al. RSS 2024) is a hand-held, 3D-printed gripper with a wrist-mounted GoPro. A fisheye lens and side mirrors give a wide, implicitly stereo view; visual-inertial SLAM recovers the gripper’s 6-DoF trajectory; and the policy interface accounts for latency differences between data collection and deployment. Because the observation (wrist camera) and action (end-effector pose, gripper width) are the same on the hand-held device and on the robot, data collected in kitchens and parks transfers to real arms. The same principle, make the data interface and the robot interface identical, recurs throughout embodied AI.

Practical tips that matter more than the architecture: consistent demonstrators, calibrated cameras, synchronised timestamps, recording the controller’s actual targets (not the measured state), and collecting recovery behaviour on purpose.

5. Large datasets and cross-embodiment learning

Single-lab datasets have hundreds to tens of thousands of episodes. Pooling data across labs and robots is the robotics version of web-scale pre-training:

  • Open X-Embodiment (ICRA 2024): a collaboration of 21 institutions that standardized datasets from 22 robots, covering 527 skills (160,266 tasks), into the RLDS format. RT-1-X and RT-2-X trained on the mixture outperformed single-robot policies; on the authors’ evaluation RT-2-X showed about three times the success of RT-2 on emergent skills.
  • BridgeData V2 (CoRL 2023): tabletop manipulation with a low-cost WidowX arm across many environments; a common pre-training and evaluation set.
  • DROID (RSS 2024): 76k teleoperated trajectories (about 350 hours) on Franka arms in 564 scenes, collected by many institutions to maximize scene diversity.
  • LeRobot (Hugging Face): a PyTorch library and data format with implementations of ACT, Diffusion Policy and VLA models (including SmolVLA and pi0), plus a hub of community datasets recorded on low-cost arms.

Cross-embodiment training raises its own questions: how to align action spaces (end-effector deltas vs. joints), how to handle different camera setups, and how to weight datasets. Post 5 discusses how VLA models answer them.

6. A runnable Diffusion Policy training step

The script below implements the core of Diffusion Policy on a toy problem that exposes multimodality: demonstrations start near the origin and move forward while bending either left or right around an obstacle. It trains a noise-prediction network over 8-step action chunks with a cosine DDPM schedule and, for comparison, an MSE behavior cloning model. The denoiser is a small MLP (the paper uses a 1-D temporal U-Net or a transformer), but the training step and the sampler are the real thing. It runs in about half a minute on a CPU.

import math
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
H, A, O = 8, 2, 2          # action horizon (chunk length), action dim, observation dim
K = 100                    # diffusion steps

# ---- toy demonstrations: from the start, go around an obstacle either left OR right ----
def make_demos(n):
    obs = torch.randn(n, O) * 0.05                       # start position near the origin
    side = torch.randint(0, 2, (n, 1)).float() * 2 - 1   # -1 = left, +1 = right (multimodal!)
    t = torch.linspace(0, 1, H)
    x = t.expand(n, H)                                   # move forward in x
    y = side * torch.sin(math.pi * t) * 0.5              # bend left or right in y
    act = torch.stack([x, y], -1) + obs[:, None, :]      # [n, H, 2] chunk of future waypoints
    return obs, act

# ---- noise schedule (DDPM, cosine) ----
s = 0.008
f = torch.cos((torch.arange(K + 1) / K + s) / (1 + s) * math.pi / 2) ** 2
alpha_bar = (f / f[0])[1:]                               # \bar{alpha}_k, k = 1..K
alphas = alpha_bar / torch.cat([torch.ones(1), alpha_bar[:-1]])
betas = (1 - alphas).clamp(max=0.999)

class NoisePredictor(nn.Module):
    """eps_theta(a_k, k, o): an MLP over the flattened action chunk (a 1-D U-Net in the paper)."""
    def __init__(self, hidden=256):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(H * A + O + 32, hidden), nn.Mish(),
                                 nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.Mish(),
                                 nn.Linear(hidden, H * A))
    def forward(self, a_noisy, k, obs):
        freqs = torch.exp(torch.arange(16) * (-math.log(1000.0) / 16))
        emb = k[:, None].float() * freqs[None]                     # sinusoidal step embedding
        emb = torch.cat([emb.sin(), emb.cos()], -1)
        x = torch.cat([a_noisy.flatten(1), obs, emb], -1)
        return self.net(x).view(-1, H, A)

def train_step(model, opt, obs, act):
    """One Diffusion Policy training step: predict the noise added to an action chunk."""
    B = act.shape[0]
    k = torch.randint(0, K, (B,))                                   # random diffusion step
    eps = torch.randn_like(act)
    ab = alpha_bar[k].view(B, 1, 1)
    a_noisy = ab.sqrt() * act + (1 - ab).sqrt() * eps               # forward process q(a_k | a_0)
    loss = F.mse_loss(model(a_noisy, k, obs), eps)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return loss.item()

@torch.no_grad()
def sample(model, obs):
    """DDPM reverse process: start from Gaussian noise, denoise K times."""
    a = torch.randn(obs.shape[0], H, A)
    for k in reversed(range(K)):
        kk = torch.full((obs.shape[0],), k)
        eps = model(a, kk, obs)
        a = (a - betas[k] / (1 - alpha_bar[k]).sqrt() * eps) / alphas[k].sqrt()
        if k > 0:
            a = a + betas[k].sqrt() * torch.randn_like(a)
    return a

if __name__ == "__main__":
    model = NoisePredictor()
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-6)
    bc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(O, 256), nn.Mish(), nn.Linear(256, H * A))   # MSE baseline
    opt_bc = torch.optim.Adam(bc.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    for it in range(3000):
        obs, act = make_demos(256)
        loss = train_step(model, opt, obs, act)
        l_bc = F.mse_loss(bc(obs).view(-1, H, A), act)
        opt_bc.zero_grad(); l_bc.backward(); opt_bc.step()
        if it % 1000 == 0:
            print(f"it {it}: diffusion loss {loss:.4f}, BC loss {l_bc.item():.4f}")
    obs = torch.zeros(1000, O)
    mid_dp = sample(model, obs)[:, H // 2, 1]           # lateral offset in the middle of the chunk
    with torch.no_grad():
        mid_bc = bc(obs).view(-1, H, A)[:, H // 2, 1]
    print("diffusion: fraction left %.2f, right %.2f, mean |y| %.3f" %
          ((mid_dp < -0.25).float().mean(), (mid_dp > 0.25).float().mean(), mid_dp.abs().mean()))
    print("MSE BC:    mean y %.3f (collapses to the average, i.e. into the obstacle)" % mid_bc.mean())

Output:

it 0: diffusion loss 1.0366, BC loss 0.2291
it 1000: diffusion loss 0.0401, BC loss 0.0542
it 2000: diffusion loss 0.0299, BC loss 0.0547
diffusion: fraction left 0.56, right 0.43, mean |y| 0.484
MSE BC:    mean y 0.022 (collapses to the average, i.e. into the obstacle)

Recording the intermediate chunks of sample shows how the two modes emerge from noise:

The diffusion policy samples both modes in roughly the demonstrated 50/50 proportion, with a lateral offset close to the true $0.5 \sin(\pi \cdot 4/7) \approx 0.49$ at the middle of the chunk, while MSE BC predicts $y \approx 0$: straight through the obstacle. Its loss also plateaus near 0.055, about the variance of the two modes it averages. To turn this into a real policy: replace obs with image features from a ResNet or ViT (trained end-to-end with random-crop augmentation), use a temporal U-Net, normalize actions to $[-1, 1]$, keep an exponential moving average of the weights for evaluation, and execute the first $T_a$ actions of each sampled chunk in a receding-horizon loop. LeRobot’s implementation is a good reference.

7. Beyond plain imitation

  • Inverse RL and adversarial imitation. Recover a reward that explains the demonstrations, then optimize it. GAIL (Ho and Ermon 2016) trains a discriminator between expert and policy state-action pairs and uses it as a reward; adversarial motion priors in character animation follow the same idea.
  • Offline RL uses rewards on fixed datasets to improve beyond the demonstrator.
  • Learning from play and language. Unstructured teleoperation “play” data relabeled with goals or language instructions (CALVIN) feeds language-conditioned policies, the step from IL to VLA models.

Try it

None of the home-page demos is an imitation learner, but the Lab cloth demo makes a good thought experiment: dragging the cloth with the mouse is a “demonstration” of a deformable-object manipulation trajectory. Recording the mouse path and the particle positions would give exactly the $(o_t, a_t)$ pairs that a cloth-folding policy is trained on.

2025-2026 update (as of November 2026)

Three developments since early 2026 change how this post’s ideas are used in practice. Datasets are now counted in thousands of hours rather than thousands of episodes. Handheld UMI-style collection has grown into a data source large enough to pre-train foundation models. And “Large Behavior Models”, Diffusion-Policy-style models trained on many tasks, have been evaluated with unusual statistical care. Statuses are as of November 2026.

Datasets: the numbers

The table collects figures stated in each paper or on its official page. Different datasets count different things (trajectories, hours, scenes), so compare within a column, not across columns.

Dataset Status Size Embodiments Diversity
BridgeData V2 CoRL 2023 60,096 trajectories 1 (WidowX 250) 24 environments, 13 skills
Open X-Embodiment ICRA 2024 1M+ trajectories from 60 datasets 22 robot types 527 skills, 21 institutions
DROID RSS 2024 76k trajectories, 350 h 1 (Franka) 564 scenes, 86 tasks
RoboMIND RSS 2025 about 107k trajectories 4 479 tasks, includes 5k failure demos
AgiBot World arXiv preprint (Mar 2025) 1M+ trajectories AgiBot G1 platform 217 tasks, 5 deployment scenarios
Galaxea Open-World arXiv preprint (Aug 2025) 500+ h 1 (R1 Lite mobile manipulator) 11 real sites (homes, shops, …)
TRI LBM pre-training mix Science Robotics 2026 about 1,700 h (468 h own teleoperation, 45 h sim, 32 h UMI, about 1,150 h OXE) several 29 evaluation tasks
Being-H0.5 / UniHand-2.0 arXiv preprint (Jan 2026) 35,000+ h, mostly human hand interaction human + 30 robot embodiments human-centric pre-training
Bimanual household data (Xu et al.) arXiv preprint (Sep 2026) 1,500 h (open-sourced) bimanual expert data plus on-policy corrections

Two trends stand out. First, diversity of scenes beats repetition. DROID’s 564 scenes and Galaxea’s real homes and shops are designed for the generalization axes of post 5. Second, the largest numbers now come from human data. UniHand-2.0 and EgoScale (post 6) are measured in tens of thousands of hours, an order of magnitude more than any robot-teleoperation corpus. The 2026 paper by Xu et al. adds a useful twist: it scales DAgger-style on-policy correction data (section 1) alongside expert demonstrations and studies how both scale. Covariate shift is still the enemy at 1,500 hours.

UMI-style collection grows up

The handheld gripper of section 4 has become a family:

  • UMI on Legs (Ha et al., arXiv preprint, July 2024) runs UMI-trained manipulation policies on a quadruped through a whole-body controller trained in simulation. The policy outputs end-effector targets in a world frame, so it does not care what carries the gripper.
  • FastUMI (Zhaxizhuoma et al., arXiv preprint, September 2024) replaces UMI’s visual SLAM with off-the-shelf tracking, which makes the hardware easier to reproduce, and releases more than 10k trajectories.
  • DexUMI (Xu et al., CoRL 2025) uses the human hand as the interface. An exoskeleton matches the robot hand’s kinematics, and the human hand is inpainted into the robot hand in the video, which closes the visual gap.
  • ViTaMIn (Liu et al., arXiv preprint, April 2025) and its bimanual successor add tactile sensing to the handheld gripper. UMI-FT (Choi et al., arXiv preprint, January 2026) adds a 6-axis force-torque sensor per finger for compliant, contact-rich tasks.
  • RDT2 (Liu et al., ICML 2026) is the scale test. It trains a 7B VLA on more than 10k hours of UMI data and deploys it zero-shot on robots it never saw (post 5).

Diffusion and flow policies: faster and smoother

  • Real-time chunking (Black et al., NeurIPS 2025) fixes the pause and jerk at chunk boundaries of the action chunking in section 2. The next chunk is generated while the current one executes, by inpainting with the committed actions frozen. A follow-up moves this conditioning into training.
  • Streaming Flow Policy (Jiang et al., CoRL 2025) treats the action trajectory itself as the flow trajectory, so actions can be streamed to the robot while sampling is still running.
  • One-Step Flow Policy (Li et al., arXiv preprint, March 2026) self-distils a flow policy into a single network evaluation. On 56 simulated tasks it matches or beats 100-step diffusion and flow policies at more than 100 times the speed. This is distillation taken to its limit: one network evaluation per action chunk.

Large Behavior Models

A careful examination of large behavior models for multitask dexterous manipulation (TRI LBM Team, arXiv July 2025; published in Science Robotics in 2026 according to the project page) pre-trains Diffusion-Policy-style transformers on the roughly 1,700-hour mix in the table above, then fine-tunes them on new tasks. Its most useful contribution for a learner is methodological. Evaluation is blind and randomized, uses about 1,800 real-world and 47k simulated rollouts, and reports confidence intervals. Under this protocol, multitask pre-training made fine-tuned policies more successful and more robust, and new tasks needed only a fraction of the data of single-task baselines. Performance also rose as pre-training data grew in scale and diversity. Exercise 5 of post 5 asks you to design exactly such a protocol.

Boston Dynamics and TRI then trained an LBM for the electric Atlas humanoid. According to the 2025 Boston Dynamics blog post, it is a roughly 450M-parameter diffusion transformer trained with flow matching. It outputs 48-step action chunks at 30 Hz (executing 24 before replanning) for the whole body, hands and feet included. It is the action chunking of section 2 at humanoid scale.

What changed since the earlier sections: section 5 described datasets in trajectories. For 2026-scale corpora, hours and number of distinct scenes are the more informative units, and human data has overtaken robot data in raw size.

Learning resources

  • LeRobot: datasets, ACT, Diffusion Policy and VLA implementations, tutorials for low-cost arms.
  • Diffusion Policy code and project page, with Colab notebooks.
  • ACT / ALOHA code and the UMI project page.
  • robomimic: benchmark and reference implementations for offline imitation.
  • R. Tedrake, Robotic Manipulation, chapter on imitation learning.
  • S. Levine, CS 285 lectures on imitation learning and DAgger.

Exercises

  1. Reproduce the compounding-error effect: train MSE BC on noise-free demonstrations of a 1-D point tracking a sinusoid, roll it out with small observation noise, and plot error versus horizon. Then add DAgger with a scripted expert.
  2. In the diffusion script, replace the MLP with a 1-D convolutional U-Net with FiLM conditioning and compare sample quality for $H = 16$.
  3. Implement DDIM sampling with 10 steps and measure how the left/right fractions and the trajectory quality change.
  4. Replace the diffusion objective by flow matching: sample $t\sim U(0,1)$, set $A^t = (1-t)\epsilon + t A^0$ and regress the velocity $A^0 - \epsilon$; sample by integrating the ODE with 10 Euler steps.
  5. Implement ACT-style temporal ensembling on top of the diffusion sampler (query every step, average overlapping predictions with exponential weights) and compare smoothness with receding-horizon execution.

  6. Dataset scale (update section): convert the hours in the dataset-scale figure to frames at 30 fps for EgoScale (20,854 h) and DROID (350 h). Why does the raw ratio overstate how much more useful the human data is for a robot?

    Hint

    $20{,}854 \cdot 3600 \cdot 30 \approx 2.25\times 10^9$ frames against $350 \cdot 3600 \cdot 30 \approx 3.8\times 10^7$, a ratio of about 60. But human video has no robot actions: the actions must be estimated (hand poses, retargeting), the body and the camera differ from the robot’s, and many frames show no manipulation. Papers therefore mix it with a much smaller amount of robot data and report scaling trends, not one-to-one exchange rates.

Next: Vision-Language-Action models, where imitation learning meets foundation models.
entry.summary: Learning robot skills from demonstrations: covariate shift and DAgger, action chunking with transformers (ACT/ALOHA), Diffusion Policy, data collection with teleoperation and UMI, and large cross-embodiment datasets, with a runnable diffusion-policy training example.

entry.title: Simulation platforms for embodied AI: MuJoCo, Isaac, Habitat, ManiSkill, Genesis

link.title: Simulation platforms for embodied AI: MuJoCo, Isaac, Habitat, ManiSkill, Genesis

entry.content:
Why this matters

The RL post ended with policies that learn to walk in minutes, but only because thousands of copies of the robot were simulated in parallel. Simulators are to embodied AI what datasets are to computer vision: they generate the training data, define the benchmarks, and their errors become the reality gap. They are also where robotics meets computer graphics most directly. A modern simulator is a game engine with a stricter physics core, and the techniques of the graphics track (rasterization, ray tracing, BVHs, position-based dynamics) are its building blocks. This post explains what a simulator computes, compares the major platforms, and walks through MuJoCo in Python.

Prerequisites

  • Posts 1 and 2 (equations of motion, PD control, RL training loops).
  • Basic numerical integration (explicit and semi-implicit Euler).
  • Optional: the graphics track’s posts on rasterization, ray tracing and physics simulation.

1. What a robotics simulator does

Every simulator repeats the same loop at a fixed time step $\Delta t$ (typically 1 to 5 ms), usually several “substeps” per control step:

flowchart LR
  A[Policy / controller] -->|ctrl| B[Actuator models]
  B --> C[Collision detection]
  C --> D[Constraint and contact solve]
  D --> E[Integrate q, v]
  E --> F[Sensors: joints, IMU, force, touch]
  E --> G[Rendering: RGB, depth, segmentation]
  F --> A
  G --> A

On a time axis, the loop looks like this for a typical setup with a 50 Hz policy and a 2 ms physics step:

Rigid-body dynamics

Most robotics engines use generalized (reduced) coordinates: the state is the joint vector $q$ and its velocity $v$, and the dynamics are the manipulator equation from post 1,

\[M(q)\,\dot v + c(q, v) = \tau + J_c(q)^\top f_c ,\]

where $c$ collects Coriolis, centrifugal and gravity terms and $J_c^\top f_c$ maps contact forces into joint space. Joints are satisfied exactly by construction, and $M$, $c$ are computed with the $O(n)$ algorithms of Featherstone (CRBA, RNEA, ABA). MuJoCo, Drake, Pinocchio, RaiSim and PhysX articulations work this way. Game engines and many graphics solvers instead use maximal coordinates: every body has its own 6-DoF pose and joints are constraints between bodies. That is simpler and parallelizes well, but joint constraints drift and long chains converge slowly.

Integration is usually semi-implicit (symplectic) Euler, $v_{t+1} = v_t + \Delta t\,\dot v_t$, then $q_{t+1} = q_t \oplus \Delta t\, v_{t+1}$ (where $\oplus$ handles quaternions for free joints). MuJoCo also offers implicit integration of damping terms and an RK4 integrator; stiff joints and actuators often require the implicit options.

Why semi-implicit Euler? The figure integrates a pendulum with a deliberately large step. Explicit Euler pumps energy into the system, semi-implicit (symplectic) Euler keeps it bounded at the same cost per step, and RK4 is accurate but needs four force evaluations per step:

Contacts and friction

Contacts are where simulators differ the most and where most sim-to-real problems come from.

  1. Collision detection. A broad phase (bounding-volume hierarchies or sweep-and-prune, exactly the BVH ideas used in ray tracing) finds candidate pairs; a narrow phase computes contact points, normals and penetration depths for convex shapes with GJK/EPA or MPR, or with analytic formulas for primitive pairs (sphere-plane, capsule-capsule). Non-convex meshes are usually decomposed into convex pieces (e.g. V-HACD, CoACD) or approximated with SDFs.

  2. Contact model. For a contact with normal impulse $\lambda_n$ and gap $\phi(q)$ the ideal rigid model is the complementarity condition

    \[0 \le \lambda_n \;\perp\; \phi(q) \ge 0 ,\]

    i.e. either the bodies touch and push, or they separate and the force is zero. Coulomb friction adds a friction cone $\lVert \lambda_t \rVert \le \mu \lambda_n$ together with maximal dissipation. Solving this exactly gives a (nonlinear) complementarity problem per step, often linearized with a pyramidal friction cone into an LCP (Stewart and Trinkle 1996; Anitescu and Potra 1997) and solved with projected Gauss-Seidel (PGS).

  3. MuJoCo’s approach (Todorov, ICRA 2014) relaxes hard complementarity into a convex optimization: constraint forces minimize a quadratic objective subject to friction-cone constraints, with a small amount of softness controlled by the solref and solimp parameters. Convexity gives a unique solution and smooth, invertible dynamics (useful for optimization and estimation) at the cost of small penetrations and slip. You saw a 0.1 mm penetration in the example below.

  4. Position-based approaches. PBD and XPBD (Macklin et al. 2016) skip forces altogether and directly project positions onto constraints. XPBD adds a compliance $\alpha$ so stiffness is independent of the iteration count: for a constraint $C(x) = 0$ with $\tilde\alpha = \alpha / \Delta t^2$, each iteration updates the Lagrange multiplier and positions as

    \[\Delta\lambda = \frac{-C(x) - \tilde\alpha\,\lambda}{\nabla C\, M^{-1}\nabla C^\top + \tilde\alpha}, \qquad \Delta x = M^{-1}\nabla C^\top \Delta\lambda .\]

    This is what the cloth demo on the home page runs, and it is the basis of NVIDIA’s Flex and of cloth, rope and soft-body simulation in Isaac and Genesis.

Practical consequences: contact parameters (friction, restitution, softness) are among the most important things to randomize; small time steps help more than many solver iterations; and grasping with thin objects or many contacts (cloth, granular media, cables) remains hard everywhere.

The two contact conditions are easiest to understand as shapes: an L-shaped set for the normal direction and a cone for friction.

The XPBD claim, stiffness independent of the iteration count, can be checked directly with the update formula above:

Actuators and sensors

A real joint is not an ideal torque source. Simulators model actuators: DC motors with gear ratios, armature (reflected rotor inertia, which strongly stabilizes small fast joints), joint damping and friction, torque and velocity limits, position servos with gains, and sometimes learned actuator networks (post 2). Sensors read the state with noise and latency: joint encoders, IMUs (accelerometer and gyro of a site), force/torque sensors, touch sensors on geoms, and cameras.

Rendering

Vision-based policies need images. Options trade speed for realism:

Renderer Examples Use
Rasterization (OpenGL/Vulkan) MuJoCo, SAPIEN, PyBullet, Habitat-Sim fast RGB-D and segmentation, millions of frames
Batched GPU renderers ManiSkill3, Madrona, MJX/MJWarp batch renderers thousands of cameras in parallel for visual RL
Real-time ray/path tracing Isaac Sim (RTX), SAPIEN ray tracer, Genesis photorealistic data, synthetic data generation
Neural / Gaussian-splatting scenes SplatSim, RoboGSim, Real-is-Sim (research) photoreal digital twins reconstructed from real scans

The last row is where the neural-rendering track meets robotics: 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructs a real workspace from a phone video, and the simulator renders the robot and objects inside it, which can shrink the visual sim-to-real gap.

Scene and robot description formats

  • URDF (ROS): links, joints, inertias, visual and collision meshes; widely supported but tree-only and with no actuators or sensors beyond extensions.
  • MJCF (MuJoCo): richer, including actuators, tendons, sensors, equality constraints and defaults.
  • USD (Pixar’s Universal Scene Description, used by Omniverse/Isaac Sim): full scenes with materials and physics schemas. The graphics pipeline’s scene graph format becomes the robot’s world.

Collections such as MuJoCo Menagerie provide curated, tested models of many commercial robots.

2. The platform landscape

Platform Physics Strengths Typical use
MuJoCo (Google DeepMind, open source since 2022) generalized coords, convex soft contacts accurate, fast on CPU, MJX (JAX) and MuJoCo Warp (GPU) variants, MuJoCo Playground control research, locomotion, dexterous hands, model-based RL
Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab (NVIDIA) PhysX 5 on GPU, RTX rendering, USD massive parallelism, photoreal sensors, large robot library sim-to-real locomotion and manipulation, synthetic data
Habitat (Meta) Bullet-based, focus on rendering speed thousands of FPS in scanned 3D homes (Matterport, HM3D), humans and avatars in 3.0 navigation, rearrangement, embodied QA, human-robot collaboration
SAPIEN / ManiSkill (UCSD, Hillbot) PhysX, GPU-parallel in ManiSkill3 articulated objects (PartNet-Mobility), fast batched rendering, many tasks manipulation benchmarks, visual RL, imitation
Genesis (open-source consortium, 2024) multi-solver: rigid, MPM, SPH, FEM, PBD many material types in one engine, Python-native, generative data engine planned soft bodies, fluids, research prototyping
Drake (TRI/MIT) hydroelastic contact, optimization tools rigorous modelling, trajectory optimization, systems framework model-based control and planning
PyBullet Bullet, maximal + reduced coords simple, ubiquitous in older papers teaching, legacy baselines
Newton (NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, Disney Research; Linux Foundation, 2025) GPU, built on NVIDIA Warp, includes MuJoCo Warp extensible differentiable physics next-generation robot learning

A few specifics worth knowing:

  • Isaac Gym (Makoviychuk et al. 2021) first showed end-to-end GPU simulation and training with tensors that never leave the GPU. It evolved into Orbit (Mittal et al. 2023) and then Isaac Lab, built on Isaac Sim.
  • MJX reimplements MuJoCo in JAX so a whole batch of worlds can be vmapped and jitted onto a GPU or TPU, and is differentiable; MuJoCo Warp is a newer GPU implementation that scales better on contact-rich scenes. MuJoCo Playground (2025) packages locomotion and manipulation environments with sim-to-real recipes on top of them.
  • Habitat optimizes for rendering throughput in photorealistic scanned interiors, which matters for navigation, where physics is simple but images are everything.
  • ManiSkill3 focuses on GPU-parallel simulation and rendering for manipulation, including heterogeneous scenes per environment.

3. Differentiable simulation

If the simulator is differentiable, $\partial s_{t+1}/\partial s_t$ and $\partial s_{t+1}/\partial a_t$ are available, and a policy can be trained by backpropagating through the rollout (analytic policy gradients):

\[\nabla_\theta \sum_{t} r(s_t, a_t), \qquad s_{t+1} = f(s_t, \pi_\theta(s_t)) .\]

Frameworks include Brax (JAX), MJX, DiffTaichi, NVIDIA Warp, and Genesis. In practice contact makes gradients discontinuous or misleading (a tiny change can switch a contact on and produce a huge gradient, or a resting contact can produce zero gradient), and long horizons produce exploding gradients, just as in RNNs. SHAC (Xu et al. ICLR 2022) mitigates this by truncating the rollout into short windows and bootstrapping with a learned critic. Differentiable simulation is most compelling for system identification (fitting friction and mass to real trajectories), soft bodies and cloth, and inverse design; for contact-rich locomotion, sampling-based RL with massive parallelism usually still wins.

A bouncing ball is enough to see why contact gradients mislead. The loss is the squared distance between the ball’s height after 1 s and a target, as a function of its initial velocity:

4. Benchmarks

Benchmark Simulator Focus
Meta-World (Yu et al. CoRL 2019) MuJoCo 50 tabletop tasks for multi-task and meta-RL
robosuite (Zhu et al. 2020) MuJoCo modular manipulation tasks; used by robomimic
RLBench (James et al. RA-L 2020) CoppeliaSim 100 tasks with demonstrations, vision-based
Habitat ObjectNav / Rearrange (Savva et al. 2019; Szot et al. 2021) Habitat navigation and home rearrangement
CALVIN (Mees et al. RA-L 2022) PyBullet long-horizon language-conditioned manipulation
ManiSkill2 / ManiSkill3 (Gu et al. ICLR 2023; Tao et al. 2024) SAPIEN generalizable manipulation, GPU-parallel
BEHAVIOR-1K (Li et al. CoRL 2022) OmniGibson (Isaac Sim) 1,000 everyday household activities
LIBERO (Liu et al. NeurIPS 2023) robosuite lifelong learning, standard for VLA evaluation
SimplerEnv (Li et al. CoRL 2024) SAPIEN simulated evaluation of real-world policies (RT-1, Octo, OpenVLA)

A recurring lesson: simulated success rates correlate with real ones only if the simulation was built and validated for that purpose. SimplerEnv explicitly measures that correlation, and it is a good habit to ask of any benchmark.

5. Hands-on: MuJoCo in Python

pip install mujoco gives the engine plus Python bindings. The example defines a 2-link arm and a free box in MJCF, holds the arm at a target with PD control plus bias compensation, and inspects contacts.

import mujoco
import numpy as np

XML = """
<mujoco model="arm_and_box">
  <option timestep="0.002" gravity="0 0 -9.81"/>
  <worldbody>
    <light pos="0 0 3"/>
    <geom name="floor" type="plane" size="2 2 0.1"/>
    <body name="link1" pos="0 0 0.5">
      <joint name="shoulder" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0" damping="0.5"/>
      <geom type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.5 0 0" size="0.04" mass="1"/>
      <body name="link2" pos="0.5 0 0">
        <joint name="elbow" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0" damping="0.5"/>
        <geom type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.4 0 0" size="0.035" mass="0.6"/>
        <site name="ee" pos="0.4 0 0"/>
      </body>
    </body>
    <body name="box" pos="0.6 0.4 0.3">
      <freejoint/>
      <geom name="box" type="box" size="0.05 0.05 0.05" mass="0.2" friction="0.8 0.005 0.0001"/>
    </body>
  </worldbody>
  <actuator>
    <motor name="m_shoulder" joint="shoulder" gear="1" ctrlrange="-30 30"/>
    <motor name="m_elbow" joint="elbow" gear="1" ctrlrange="-30 30"/>
  </actuator>
  <sensor>
    <jointpos joint="shoulder"/>
    <jointpos joint="elbow"/>
    <framepos objtype="site" objname="ee"/>
  </sensor>
</mujoco>
"""

model = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(XML)
data = mujoco.MjData(model)
print("nq", model.nq, "nv", model.nv, "nu", model.nu)   # 2 hinges + 1 free joint: nq=9, nv=8

q_ref = np.array([-0.6, 1.2])                # shoulder, elbow targets (rad)
Kp, Kd = 60.0, 4.0
arm = [model.joint("shoulder").qposadr[0], model.joint("elbow").qposadr[0]]
arm_v = [model.joint("shoulder").dofadr[0], model.joint("elbow").dofadr[0]]

for step in range(1500):                     # 3 s of simulated time
    q, qd = data.qpos[arm], data.qvel[arm_v]
    # PD + gravity/Coriolis compensation: qfrc_bias holds C(q,qd) qd + g(q)
    data.ctrl[:] = Kp * (q_ref - q) - Kd * qd + data.qfrc_bias[arm_v]
    mujoco.mj_step(model, data)

print("joint error", np.round(q_ref - data.qpos[arm], 4))
print("end-effector (sensor)", np.round(data.sensordata[2:5], 3))
print("box height", round(data.body("box").xpos[2], 4))   # resting on the floor at 0.05

# inspect contacts: which geoms touch and with what normal force
f = np.zeros(6)
for i in range(data.ncon):
    c = data.contact[i]
    mujoco.mj_contactForce(model, data, i, f)  # f[0] = normal force in the contact frame
    g1, g2 = model.geom(c.geom1).name, model.geom(c.geom2).name
    print(f"contact {g1}-{g2}: depth {c.dist:+.5f} m, normal force {f[0]:.3f} N")

Output (MuJoCo 3.3.7):

nq 9 nv 8 nu 2
joint error [0. 0.]
end-effector (sensor) [0.743 0.    0.556]
box height 0.0499
contact floor-box: depth -0.00011 m, normal force 0.490 N
contact floor-box: depth -0.00011 m, normal force 0.490 N
contact floor-box: depth -0.00011 m, normal force 0.491 N
contact floor-box: depth -0.00011 m, normal force 0.491 N

Things to notice:

  • nq = 9 but nv = 8: the free joint stores a position and a quaternion (7 numbers) but has only 6 velocity DoFs. Always index with qposadr and dofadr rather than assuming they match.
  • qfrc_bias is exactly $c(q, v)$, so the controller is the “PD + gravity compensation” law from post 1, and the joint error goes to zero.
  • The box rests on four contact points, whose normal forces sum to $4 \times 0.49 \approx 1.96$ N $= 0.2\,\text{kg}\times 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$. The small negative depth (0.1 mm penetration) is MuJoCo’s soft contact at work.
  • To see the scene, run python -m mujoco.viewer and load a file, or call mujoco.viewer.launch_passive(model, data) inside the loop. For offscreen images (e.g. camera observations) use mujoco.Renderer(model, 240, 320), which needs an OpenGL backend such as EGL on headless machines (MUJOCO_GL=egl).

Recording the state inside the loop and plotting it shows the same run in space and time:

Batched simulation with MJX

The same model runs as a batch of worlds on an accelerator with MJX (pip install mujoco-mjx). Save the example above as arm_and_box.py and:

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import mujoco
from mujoco import mjx

from arm_and_box import XML                  # the MJCF string from the previous example

model = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(XML)
mx = mjx.put_model(model)                    # copy the model to the accelerator

def rollout(qpos0):
    d = mjx.make_data(mx).replace(qpos=qpos0)
    def body(d, _):
        return mjx.step(mx, d), None
    d, _ = jax.lax.scan(body, d, None, length=500)
    return d.qpos

# 1024 worlds whose shoulder angle starts at different values
qpos0 = jnp.tile(jnp.array(model.qpos0), (1024, 1))
qpos0 = qpos0.at[:, 0].set(jnp.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, 1024))
final = jax.jit(jax.vmap(rollout))(qpos0)
print(final.shape)                           # (1024, 9)

vmap turns the single-world step into a batched one and jit compiles it; on a GPU this is the pattern behind “train a locomotion policy in minutes”. Because mjx.step is written in JAX, jax.grad through rollout also works, which is the differentiable-simulation use case above (with the caveats about contact gradients). Importing arm_and_box also runs its CPU simulation once, which is harmless here.

What the batch computes is easy to picture. Without a GPU, the same experiment can be run on the CPU by looping over independent MjData objects, which is exactly what vmap vectorizes:

6. Choosing a simulator

  • Locomotion, sim-to-real, many robots in parallel: Isaac Lab, MuJoCo Playground (MJX / MuJoCo Warp), Genesis.
  • Dexterous or precise contact, model-based control, system identification: MuJoCo, Drake.
  • Visual manipulation benchmarks and imitation learning: ManiSkill3, robosuite/robomimic, LIBERO, RLBench.
  • Navigation and home-scale tasks with people: Habitat 3.0, BEHAVIOR-1K (OmniGibson).
  • Deformables, fluids, cloth: Genesis, Isaac Sim (PBD/FEM), dedicated XPBD or MPM code.

Whatever you choose, validate the parts that matter for your task against the real robot: drop tests, swing tests, recorded joint trajectories, and a few real rollouts of the trained policy.

Try it

Open the Lab on the home page and switch to the Cloth · XPBD tab: a 40 x 40 particle cloth simulated with XPBD and many substeps. Pull it, cut it, stretch it until it tears. Every update you see is the $\Delta\lambda$ formula above applied to distance constraints. Notice that more substeps make the cloth stiffer and more stable; that is the same reason robotics simulators prefer small time steps. Neighbouring tabs show the rendering side: a path tracer and a Gaussian-splatting world.

2025-2026 update (as of November 2026)

Simulators change faster than papers, so this section starts with versions. Every version and date below was read from the project’s GitHub release page or an official announcement in late October 2026. ICRA 2026 (June, Vienna), RSS 2026 (July, Sydney) and IROS 2026 (September-October, Pittsburgh) have taken place. CoRL 2026 (9-12 November, Austin) and Humanoids 2026 (December, Santa Clara) are still ahead. For how a game-style physics pipeline (broad phase, narrow phase, solver) maps onto these robot simulators, and for OpenUSD and synthetic data, see the companion post Physics and simulation engines.

The GPU stacks converge: Isaac Lab 3, Newton, MuJoCo Warp

Project Latest release (Nov 2026) What changed in 2025-2026
Isaac Lab v3.0.0 (2026-10-20) multi-backend physics (PhysX or Newton) and rendering; many workflows run without Isaac Sim; quaternions now in xyzw order
Isaac Sim v6.2.0 (2026-10-14) Isaac Lab 3.0 targets this version; a 7.0 alpha is out
Newton v1.7.0 (2026-10-14) beta in September 2025, 1.0 announced at GTC in March 2026; solvers include MuJoCo Warp, Kamino (Disney), VBD deformables and implicit MPM
MuJoCo / MuJoCo Warp 3.17.0 (2026-10-22), versioned together MuJoCo Warp is the GPU backend of MuJoCo on NVIDIA hardware and one of Newton’s solvers
mjlab arXiv preprint, January 2026 Isaac Lab’s manager-based API on top of MuJoCo Warp

Three things happened. First, Isaac Lab got a reference paper (Mittal et al., arXiv preprint, November 2025). It describes the design that section 2 sketched: GPU-resident tensors, actuator models, sensors, domain randomization and RL or imitation workflows at scale. Second, Newton turned from a 2025 announcement into a released engine. It is a Linux Foundation project built on NVIDIA Warp and OpenUSD, and it hosts several solvers behind one model description, so the same robot can run with MuJoCo Warp’s soft-contact rigid bodies or with a deformable solver. Third, Isaac Lab 3.0 can now use Newton as a physics backend instead of PhysX. The line between “the NVIDIA stack” and “the MuJoCo stack” in the table of section 2 is blurring: the same environment code can switch engines. This is also a cheap robustness check, since a policy that only works in one engine is probably exploiting its contact model.

MuJoCo Playground (Zakka et al., RSS 2025, outstanding demo paper award) and mjlab (Zakka et al., arXiv preprint, January 2026) are the MuJoCo-side equivalents. Playground packages GPU environments with sim-to-real recipes for locomotion and dexterous manipulation. mjlab copies Isaac Lab’s manager API, so code moves between the two with little change.

Other platforms and benchmarks

  • Genesis: as of November 2026 the project ships 1.x releases on GitHub. We could not find an arXiv technical report, so cite the repository. Its “generative data engine” (section 2) is still described by the project as a direction, not a finished system.
  • ManiSkill3 (Tao et al., RSS 2025) and RoboVerse (Geng et al., RSS 2025). RoboVerse’s MetaSim layer runs one task definition on several simulators and ships a large synthetic dataset with imitation and RL benchmarks.
  • RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., ICLR 2026) extends RoboCasa to 365 kitchen tasks in 2,500 scenes, so a policy can be tested on a whole distribution of homes.
  • BEHAVIOR Challenge. The first edition (NeurIPS 2025, December 2025) asked teams to solve 50 full-length household activities from BEHAVIOR-1K in OmniGibson. The second edition, at CoRL 2026, has 100 tasks; submissions closed on 16 October 2026 and results are due on 4 November 2026.
  • GenManip (CVPR 2025) uses an LLM and scene graphs to generate tabletop instruction-following tasks.

Generative simulation: world models as simulators

The fourth use of world models in post 5 (policy evaluation) became concrete in 2025-2026:

  • Cosmos-Predict2.5 and Cosmos-Transfer2.5 (NVIDIA, arXiv preprint, October 2025) are open flow-based video world models at 2B and 14B parameters. The Transfer model is a control network that re-renders simulator output (depth, segmentation, edges) as photoreal video. This “sim2real augmentation” attacks the visual gap of section 1 with a generative model instead of a better renderer.
  • WorldGym (Quevedo et al., ICLR 2026) rolls out a policy inside an action-conditioned video model and scores the rollout with a VLM, which gives an approximate success rate without a robot.
  • Evaluating Gemini Robotics policies in a Veo world simulator (Gemini Robotics Team, arXiv preprint, December 2025) fine-tunes Veo on robot data and uses it to rank policies, probe out-of-distribution scenes and red-team safety, and it compares the rankings with real trials.
  • Genie 3 (Google DeepMind, blog, August 2025) generates interactive worlds in real time (720p, 24 fps, consistent for a few minutes) and was used to train and test agents. DeepMind’s Genie page now lists Genie 4 as a research preview for trusted testers and mentions early robotics uses.

The caution from section 4 applies twice over: a learned simulator is useful only after its rankings have been shown to agree with real-world rankings, and it can hallucinate success. Physics engines remain the tool for contact-rich RL. Video world models are becoming the tool for visual diversity and for cheap policy triage.

What changed since the earlier sections: the Newton row of the table in section 2 now describes a released 1.x engine, not just an announcement. Isaac Lab can run on Newton. The Genesis row stays as written.

Representative papers

Paper Venue Year Link Why it matters
Todorov, Erez, Tassa, MuJoCo: a physics engine for model-based control IROS 2012 DOI MuJoCo
Todorov, Convex and analytically-invertible dynamics with contacts and constraints: theory and implementation in MuJoCo ICRA 2014 DOI MuJoCo’s convex contact model
Macklin, Müller, Chentanez, XPBD: position-based simulation of compliant constrained dynamics MIG 2016 DOI XPBD, used by the home-page cloth demo
Savva et al., Habitat: a platform for embodied AI research ICCV 2019 arXiv Fast photoreal embodied simulation
Hu et al., DiffTaichi: differentiable programming for physical simulation ICLR 2020 arXiv Differentiable simulation language
Xiang et al., SAPIEN: a simulated part-based interactive environment CVPR 2020 arXiv Articulated-object simulation
James et al., RLBench: the robot learning benchmark and learning environment RA-L 2020 arXiv Manipulation benchmark
Makoviychuk et al., Isaac Gym: high performance GPU-based physics simulation for robot learning NeurIPS D&B 2021 arXiv End-to-end GPU simulation
Freeman et al., Brax: a differentiable physics engine for large scale rigid body simulation NeurIPS D&B 2021 arXiv JAX physics
Szot et al., Habitat 2.0: training home assistants to rearrange their habitat NeurIPS 2021 arXiv Interactive home rearrangement
Xu et al., Accelerated policy learning with parallel differentiable simulation (SHAC) ICLR 2022 arXiv Making differentiable sim useful for RL
Gu et al., ManiSkill2: a unified benchmark for generalizable manipulation skills ICLR 2023 arXiv Manipulation benchmark
Mittal et al., Orbit: a unified simulation framework for interactive robot learning environments RA-L 2023 arXiv Predecessor of Isaac Lab
Liu et al., LIBERO: benchmarking knowledge transfer for lifelong robot learning NeurIPS D&B 2023 arXiv Standard VLA benchmark
Puig et al., Habitat 3.0: a co-habitat for humans, avatars and robots ICLR 2024 arXiv Humans in the loop
Li et al., Evaluating real-world robot manipulation policies in simulation (SimplerEnv) CoRL 2024 arXiv Sim-real correlation
Tao et al., ManiSkill3: GPU parallelized robotics simulation and rendering for generalizable embodied AI RSS (demo) 2025 arXiv GPU-parallel sim and rendering
Zakka et al., MuJoCo Playground RSS (demo) 2025 arXiv MJX environments with sim-to-real recipes
Mittal et al., Isaac Lab: a GPU-accelerated simulation framework for multi-modal robot learning arXiv 2025 arXiv Isaac Lab design
Geng et al., RoboVerse: towards a unified platform, dataset and benchmark for scalable and generalizable robot learning RSS 2025 arXiv One task definition across simulators
GenManip: LLM-driven simulation for generalizable instruction-following manipulation CVPR 2025 arXiv LLM-generated tabletop tasks
Quevedo et al., WorldGym: world model as an environment for policy evaluation ICLR 2026 arXiv Video world model as evaluator
NVIDIA, World simulation with video foundation models for physical AI (Cosmos-Predict2.5 / Transfer2.5) arXiv preprint (Oct 2025) 2025 arXiv Open world models, sim2real augmentation
Mittal et al., Isaac Lab: a GPU-accelerated simulation framework for multi-modal robot learning arXiv preprint (Nov 2025) 2025 arXiv Reference paper for Isaac Lab
Gemini Robotics Team, Evaluating Gemini Robotics policies in a Veo world simulator arXiv preprint (Dec 2025) 2025 arXiv Policy ranking and safety probes in a world model
Zakka et al., mjlab: a lightweight framework for GPU-accelerated robot learning arXiv preprint (Jan 2026) 2026 arXiv Isaac Lab API on MuJoCo Warp
Nasiriany et al., RoboCasa365: a large-scale simulation framework for training and benchmarking generalist robots ICLR 2026 arXiv 365 tasks, 2,500 kitchen scenes
Software: Isaac Lab releases, Newton, MuJoCo Warp, BEHAVIOR Challenge, Genie 3 release / blog 2025-2026 see links Versions as of November 2026

Learning resources

  • MuJoCo documentation, especially the Computation chapter (dynamics, contact model, solver), the Python bindings, the MJX page and the official Colab tutorials linked from them.
  • MuJoCo Menagerie: curated robot models.
  • Isaac Lab documentation and tutorials; ManiSkill; Habitat-Lab; Genesis; Newton; MuJoCo Warp.
  • R. Tedrake, Robotic Manipulation, chapters on simulation and contact with Drake.
  • R. Featherstone, Rigid Body Dynamics Algorithms (Springer, 2008); D. Stewart, “Rigid-body dynamics with friction and impact”, SIAM Review 2000, for the complementarity view of contact.
  • M. Macklin and M. Müller’s position-based dynamics tutorials and the graphics track’s simulation post.

Exercises

  1. In the MuJoCo example, change the box friction to 0.1 and give the floor a slight tilt (rotate the plane). At what angle does the box start sliding? Compare with $\tan\theta = \mu$.
  2. Replace the motor actuators with position actuators (kp gain) and compare the tracking error with and without the qfrc_bias term. Why does a pure position servo sag?
  3. Use mujoco.Renderer to render a 64 x 64 depth image of the scene after each control step, and measure frames per second on CPU.
  4. Randomize the box mass and friction across the 1024 MJX worlds (put per-world values in a batched mjx.Model) and plot the distribution of final box positions after a push.
  5. Implement a 1-D XPBD chain (10 particles, distance constraints) in NumPy and show that increasing the iteration count changes the stiffness with plain PBD but not with XPBD.

  6. World models as simulators (update section): name two ways a learned video world model can give a wrong verdict when it is used to evaluate a policy, and design one check for each.

    Hint

    Typical failures are hallucinated success (the model renders the object in the gripper although the actions could not have grasped it), drift over long horizons, and action insensitivity (the video barely changes when the actions change). Checks: replay the same start with zero or random actions and confirm that the predicted outcome changes; and, as in the Veo evaluator work above, rank several policies in the world model and compare the ranking with real-robot results.

Next: Imitation learning: learning from demonstrations instead of rewards.
entry.summary: What a robotics simulator actually computes (dynamics, contacts, rendering, sensors), a tour of today's platforms and benchmarks, differentiable and GPU-parallel simulation, and a hands-on MuJoCo/MJX example.

entry.title: Reinforcement learning for robots: from MDPs to PPO, SAC and sim-to-real

link.title: Reinforcement learning for robots: from MDPs to PPO, SAC and sim-to-real

entry.content:
Why this matters

In the previous post every controller was designed by hand from a model. That works for an arm moving in free space, but it becomes very hard for a quadruped running over rubble or a hand spinning a cube, where contacts switch on and off hundreds of times a second. Reinforcement learning (RL) replaces the hand design by optimization: write down a reward, let the robot try millions of times in a simulator, and transfer the resulting policy to hardware. Since about 2019 this recipe has become the standard way to build locomotion controllers, and its ideas (advantages, entropy, domain randomization) show up again in imitation learning, VLA fine-tuning and world-model training later in this series.

Prerequisites

  • Post 1 of this series (joint-space PD control, action spaces).
  • Probability: expectations, the log-derivative trick, Gaussian distributions.
  • PyTorch basics (autograd, nn.Module, optimizers).
  • If you know world models: model-based RL appears in post 5 and in the world-models track; here we stay model-free.

1. The RL problem

Markov decision processes

An MDP is a tuple $(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, P, r, \gamma, \rho_0)$: states, actions, transition dynamics \(P(s' \mid s, a)\), reward $r(s, a)$, discount $\gamma \in [0, 1)$ and initial-state distribution $\rho_0$. A (stochastic) policy $\pi_\theta(a \mid s)$ induces trajectories $\tau = (s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1, \dots)$ and the objective is the expected discounted return

\[J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_\theta}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t r(s_t, a_t)\right].\]

Real robots are partially observable (POMDP): the policy sees observations $o_t$ (joint encoders, an IMU, images) rather than the full state (exact contact forces, terrain friction). Practitioners handle this with observation histories, recurrent networks, or the privileged-information tricks of section 4.

For a robot the modelling choices are as important as the algorithm:

MDP element Typical choice for a legged robot
Observation base angular velocity, projected gravity, joint positions and velocities, previous action, velocity command, (height map)
Action joint position targets $q^{\text{des}}$ for a PD loop at 200 Hz to 1 kHz; policy at 50 Hz
Reward track commanded velocity, penalize torque, joint acceleration, action rate, foot slip, base orientation
Episode 20 s, terminate on falls (base contact), randomized start state and terrain

Put together, one step of a legged-robot RL system looks like the loop in the figure: the policy runs slowly, a PD loop turns its targets into torques quickly, and batches of trajectories from many parallel environments feed the PPO update.

Value functions and the Bellman equations

The state value and action value of a policy are

\[V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\left[\sum_{k\ge 0}\gamma^k r_{t+k} \,\middle\vert\, s_t = s\right], \qquad Q^\pi(s,a) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\left[\sum_{k\ge 0}\gamma^k r_{t+k} \,\middle\vert\, s_t = s, a_t = a\right],\]

and the advantage $A^\pi(s,a) = Q^\pi(s,a) - V^\pi(s)$ measures how much better action $a$ is than the policy’s average. They satisfy the Bellman expectation equation

\[Q^\pi(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma\,\mathbb{E}_{s'\sim P,\,a'\sim\pi}\left[Q^\pi(s',a')\right],\]

and the optimal action value satisfies the Bellman optimality equation \(Q^{\ast}(s,a) = r + \gamma\,\mathbb{E}_{s'}[\max_{a'} Q^{\ast}(s',a')]\). Q-learning and DQN (Mnih et al. 2015) iterate the latter, but the $\max$ over a continuous, high-dimensional action space is awkward, which is why robotics mostly uses policy-gradient and actor-critic methods.

For a small, known MDP the Bellman optimality equation can be solved directly by value iteration, $V_{k+1}(s) = \max_a \sum_{s’} P(s’\mid s,a)\,[r + \gamma V_k(s’)]$. The figure and the widget below show how value spreads backwards from the reward, one sweep at a time.

Interactive: press Step to apply one Bellman backup to every cell, or Run to iterate until $\max\lvert\Delta V\rvert < 10^{-4}$. Click cells to add or remove walls, and change $\gamma$ or the slip probability to see how far value propagates and how cautious the greedy policy becomes.

2. Policy gradients

The policy gradient theorem

Using $\nabla_\theta p_\theta(\tau) = p_\theta(\tau)\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau)$ and the fact that the dynamics do not depend on $\theta$, one gets (Williams 1992; Sutton et al. 2000)

\[\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}\left[\sum_t \nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)\, \hat A_t\right],\]

where $\hat A_t$ can be the return-to-go (REINFORCE), the return minus a baseline $b(s_t)$, or an advantage estimate. Subtracting a state-dependent baseline does not bias the gradient but greatly reduces its variance. Intuitively, the gradient raises the log-probability of actions that turned out better than expected and lowers the others.

For continuous control the policy is usually a diagonal Gaussian $\pi_\theta(a\mid s) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\theta(s), \mathrm{diag}(\sigma^2))$ with a state-independent, learned $\log\sigma$.

A one-step problem (a bandit) makes the update visible. Samples with positive advantage pull the mean of the Gaussian toward them, samples with negative advantage push it away, and repeated steps also shrink $\sigma$ once the policy has found the optimum:

Generalized advantage estimation

With a learned critic $V_\phi$ define the TD residual $\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V_\phi(s_{t+1}) - V_\phi(s_t)$. GAE (Schulman et al. 2016) averages $k$-step advantage estimates with exponentially decaying weights:

\[\hat A_t^{\mathrm{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)} = \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} (\gamma\lambda)^l\,\delta_{t+l}.\]

$\lambda = 0$ gives the low-variance, biased one-step TD advantage; $\lambda = 1$ gives the unbiased, high-variance Monte-Carlo advantage. $\lambda \approx 0.95$ is the usual compromise. The critic is regressed to the targets $\hat R_t = \hat A_t + V_\phi(s_t)$.

The top panel shows how $\lambda$ sets the horizon over which TD residuals are averaged. The bottom panel measures the resulting trade-off on a toy chain whose critic is deliberately wrong:

Trust regions and PPO

Plain policy gradients are fragile: one large step can collapse the policy, and then the data it collects is useless. TRPO (Schulman et al. 2015) maximizes a surrogate objective subject to a KL-divergence constraint between the old and new policy. PPO (Schulman et al. 2017) gets most of the benefit with a first-order trick. With the probability ratio $\rho_t(\theta) = \pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)/\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t\mid s_t)$ it maximizes

\[L^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t\left[\min\left(\rho_t(\theta)\hat A_t,\; \operatorname{clip}(\rho_t(\theta), 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon)\,\hat A_t\right)\right],\]

usually with $\epsilon = 0.2$. The $\min$ makes this a pessimistic bound: once the ratio leaves $[1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon]$ in the direction that would improve the objective, the gradient vanishes, so there is no incentive to move further. That lets PPO reuse each batch for several epochs of minibatch SGD. The full loss adds a value loss and an optional entropy bonus:

\[L(\theta,\phi) = -L^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta) + c_v\,\mathbb{E}_t\left[(V_\phi(s_t) - \hat R_t)^2\right] - c_e\,\mathbb{E}_t\left[\mathcal{H}(\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s_t))\right].\]

PPO is on-policy and sample-inefficient, but it is simple, stable and embarrassingly parallel. With thousands of simulated robots on one GPU, sample efficiency matters much less than wall-clock time, which is why PPO is the default in Isaac Lab, legged_gym and most locomotion papers.

Plotting $L^{\text{CLIP}}$ for a single sample shows the pessimism of the $\min$: the objective is flat, and its gradient zero, exactly where moving further would look good.

A compact PPO in PyTorch

The following file is self-contained: an actor-critic, GAE, the PPO update, and a vectorized toy task in which 64 point masses must move to the origin (a stand-in for a reaching task). It runs in a few minutes on a laptop CPU.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class ActorCritic(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, obs_dim, act_dim, hidden=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.pi = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(obs_dim, hidden), nn.Tanh(),
                                nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(hidden, act_dim))
        self.v = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(obs_dim, hidden), nn.Tanh(),
                               nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(hidden, 1))
        self.log_std = nn.Parameter(torch.full((act_dim,), -0.5))

    def dist(self, obs):
        return torch.distributions.Normal(self.pi(obs), self.log_std.exp())

def gae(rew, val, done, last_val, gamma=0.99, lam=0.95):
    """rew, val, done: [T, N] tensors (N parallel envs). Returns advantages and returns."""
    T = rew.shape[0]
    adv = torch.zeros_like(rew)
    next_val, running = last_val, torch.zeros_like(last_val)
    for t in reversed(range(T)):
        mask = 1.0 - done[t]
        delta = rew[t] + gamma * next_val * mask - val[t]
        running = delta + gamma * lam * mask * running
        adv[t] = running
        next_val = val[t]
    return adv, adv + val

def ppo_update(model, opt, obs, act, logp_old, adv, ret,
               clip=0.2, vf_coef=0.5, ent_coef=0.0, epochs=10, minibatch=256):
    """One PPO update on a flattened batch of B transitions."""
    adv = (adv - adv.mean()) / (adv.std() + 1e-8)
    B = obs.shape[0]
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for idx in torch.randperm(B).split(minibatch):
            d = model.dist(obs[idx])
            logp = d.log_prob(act[idx]).sum(-1)
            ratio = (logp - logp_old[idx]).exp()
            surr = torch.min(ratio * adv[idx],
                             ratio.clamp(1 - clip, 1 + clip) * adv[idx])
            v_loss = (model.v(obs[idx]).squeeze(-1) - ret[idx]).pow(2).mean()
            loss = -surr.mean() + vf_coef * v_loss - ent_coef * d.entropy().sum(-1).mean()
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 0.5)
            opt.step()

# --- a toy "reaching" task: a 2-D point mass must move to the origin ---
class PointReach:
    def __init__(self, n, horizon=50):
        self.n, self.H = n, horizon
        self.damp, self.gain = 0.9, 0.1               # nominal physics
    def reset(self):
        self.pos = torch.rand(self.n, 2) * 2 - 1
        self.vel = torch.zeros(self.n, 2)
        self.t = torch.zeros(self.n)
        return torch.cat([self.pos, self.vel], -1)
    def step(self, a):
        a = a.clamp(-1, 1)
        self.vel = self.damp * self.vel + self.gain * a  # simple damped dynamics
        self.pos = self.pos + 0.1 * self.vel
        self.t += 1
        rew = -self.pos.norm(dim=-1) - 0.01 * a.pow(2).sum(-1)
        done = (self.t >= self.H).float()
        if done.any():                                # auto-reset finished envs
            k = done.bool()
            self.pos[k] = torch.rand(int(k.sum()), 2) * 2 - 1
            self.vel[k] = 0.0
            self.t[k] = 0
        return torch.cat([self.pos, self.vel], -1), rew, done

torch.manual_seed(0)
env, T = PointReach(n=64), 128
model = ActorCritic(4, 2)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4)
obs = env.reset()
for it in range(150):
    buf = {k: [] for k in ["obs", "act", "logp", "rew", "val", "done"]}
    with torch.no_grad():
        for t in range(T):
            d = model.dist(obs)
            a = d.sample()
            buf["obs"].append(obs); buf["act"].append(a)
            buf["logp"].append(d.log_prob(a).sum(-1))
            buf["val"].append(model.v(obs).squeeze(-1))
            obs, r, done = env.step(a)
            buf["rew"].append(r); buf["done"].append(done)
        last_val = model.v(obs).squeeze(-1)
    b = {k: torch.stack(v) for k, v in buf.items()}            # [T, N, ...]
    adv, ret = gae(b["rew"], b["val"], b["done"], last_val)
    flat = lambda x: x.reshape(T * env.n, *x.shape[2:])
    ppo_update(model, opt, flat(b["obs"]), flat(b["act"]), flat(b["logp"]), flat(adv), flat(ret))
    if it % 25 == 0 or it == 149:
        print(f"iter {it:3d}  mean reward per step {b['rew'].mean():.3f}")

On my run the mean reward per step goes from about $-0.89$ (random actions) to about $-0.1$ (the masses reach the origin and stay there). Details that matter in practice and are easy to get wrong:

  • Masking at episode ends. mask stops bootstrapping across an auto-reset. Strictly, a time-limit truncation should still bootstrap from $V(s_{T})$ (the robot did not fail, we just stopped watching); legged_gym handles this by adding $\gamma V$ of the final state to the reward on time-outs. The toy code treats time-outs as terminal, which is a small bias.
  • Advantage normalization, gradient clipping and a state-independent log-std are standard; observation normalization (running mean/variance) matters on real robots where units differ by orders of magnitude.
  • Action scaling. The network output is clamped to $[-1, 1]$ here; on a robot it is usually scaled and added to a nominal joint configuration, $q^{\text{des}} = q_0 + k_a a_t$.

Running the script above unchanged produces the learning curve in the figure, together with the behaviour of the trained policy:

3. Soft Actor-Critic

PPO throws away data after each update. Off-policy methods keep a replay buffer and are far more sample-efficient, which matters when samples come from a real robot. SAC (Haarnoja et al. 2018) optimizes the maximum-entropy objective

\[J(\pi) = \sum_t \mathbb{E}_{(s_t,a_t)\sim\pi}\left[r(s_t,a_t) + \alpha\,\mathcal{H}(\pi(\cdot\mid s_t))\right],\]

which keeps the policy as random as possible while still solving the task. This gives robust exploration and a policy that does not collapse onto one brittle solution. SAC learns two soft Q-functions $Q_{\phi_1}, Q_{\phi_2}$ (taking the minimum to fight overestimation, as in TD3) with targets

\[y = r + \gamma\left(\min_{j=1,2} Q_{\bar\phi_j}(s', \tilde a') - \alpha\log\pi_\theta(\tilde a'\mid s')\right), \qquad \tilde a' \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s'),\]

where $\bar\phi$ are slowly updated (Polyak-averaged) target networks. The actor uses the reparameterization trick with a tanh-squashed Gaussian, $\tilde a = \tanh(\mu_\theta(s) + \sigma_\theta(s)\odot\xi)$ with $\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0, I)$, and minimizes

\[L_\pi(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{D},\,\xi}\left[\alpha\log\pi_\theta(\tilde a\mid s) - \min_j Q_{\phi_j}(s, \tilde a)\right].\]

The tanh changes the density, so $\log\pi(\tilde a\mid s) = \log\mathcal{N}(u;\mu,\sigma)$ $-\, \sum_i\log(1-\tanh^2 u_i)$. The follow-up paper (Haarnoja et al. 2018b) also tunes $\alpha$ automatically toward a target entropy (often $-\dim\mathcal{A}$) and demonstrated learning to walk directly on a real Minitaur quadruped in about two hours of experience.

  PPO SAC
Data on-policy, discard after update off-policy, replay buffer
Sample efficiency low high
Parallel simulation scales very well needs care (update-to-data ratio)
Typical use sim-to-real locomotion, massively parallel sim real-world RL, manipulation, fine-tuning
Exploration Gaussian noise + optional entropy bonus maximum entropy, automatic temperature

Two pictures help with SAC. The entropy bonus turns the greedy $\arg\max_a Q$ into a Boltzmann distribution $\pi \propto \exp(Q/\alpha)$ (the optimal policy of the maximum-entropy objective in a one-step problem), and the tanh squashing needs the density correction given above:

4. Reward design

The reward is the specification of the task, and every loophole will be found. Common patterns:

  • Dense task terms (e.g. \(\exp(-\lVert v^{\text{cmd}}_{xy} - v_{xy}\rVert^2 / \sigma)\) for velocity tracking) plus many small regularization penalties (torque, power, joint acceleration, action rate $\lVert a_t - a_{t-1}\rVert^2$, foot slip, feet air time). The penalties are what make gaits look natural and transferable; without them policies vibrate, which simulators tolerate and motors do not.
  • Potential-based shaping (Ng, Harada and Russell, ICML 1999): adding \(F = \gamma\Phi(s') - \Phi(s)\) for any potential $\Phi$ provably leaves the optimal policy unchanged, while other shaping terms can change it.
  • Sparse rewards plus demonstrations or curricula for manipulation: success/failure is easy to specify but hard to explore, so one adds demonstrations (post 4), automatic curricula (terrain difficulty that increases as the policy improves, as in Rudin et al.), or goal relabeling.
  • Style rewards from data: motion imitation (DeepMimic, Peng et al. 2018) or adversarial motion priors reward the policy for looking like reference motion capture, a direct bridge from character animation to robotics.
  • LLM-written rewards: Eureka (Ma et al. 2024) asks an LLM to write reward code, trains policies in Isaac Gym, and feeds training statistics back to the LLM to refine the reward.

5. Sim-to-real transfer

Policies trained in simulation face the reality gap: wrong masses and friction, unmodelled actuator dynamics, latency, sensor noise, and images that look nothing like rendered ones. The main tools:

Domain randomization

Instead of making the simulator exactly right, make it randomly wrong in many ways, so that the real world looks like just another sample. Tobin et al. (IROS 2017) randomized textures, lighting, camera pose and distractors in a non-photorealistic renderer and trained an object detector that localized objects on a real robot to within about 1.5 cm with no real images. Peng et al. (ICRA 2018) randomized dynamics (masses, friction, damping, latency) and used a recurrent policy that can implicitly identify the current dynamics. OpenAI’s dexterous hand work (2018, 2019) pushed this to the extreme with automatic domain randomization, gradually widening the ranges as the policy succeeds.

In code, randomization is just per-environment physics parameters resampled on reset. In the toy task above:

class RandomizedPointReach(PointReach):
    """Domain randomization: every env gets its own damping and actuator gain."""
    def reset(self):
        self.damp = torch.empty(self.n, 1).uniform_(0.8, 0.97)
        self.gain = torch.empty(self.n, 1).uniform_(0.05, 0.2)
        return super().reset()

Replace PointReach(n=64) by RandomizedPointReach(n=64) and the same PPO loop learns a single policy that works across all of these “robots”. (For brevity the parameters are sampled once per reset(); a full implementation resamples them for each environment when it auto-resets.)
